Align the measurement with the objective: if the objective is to demonstrate a label calculation, counting attendance alone is insufficient. Decide who will collect the measure and how a response will be recorded.

theory.heading: A worked communication sequence
theory.text: A person receives a label stating 160 kcal per serving and plans to eat 1.5 servings. First ask what the person currently looks for on labels. Show that 160 × 1.5 = 240 kcal, labeling both the serving size and result. Invite the person to calculate a new label: 120 kcal per serving at two servings is 240 kcal. If the result is incorrect, say “I may not have explained that clearly,” show the multiplication another way, and invite another attempt. Then agree on one realistic action, such as comparing the number of servings in two usual snacks. At follow-up ask which snack was compared and what the person observed.

theory.heading: Apply, contrast, and evaluate
theory.text: Imagine two people have the same goal of preparing a lower-sodium meal. One has a kitchen and wants a practical cooking demonstration; the other relies on prepared meals and has no access to a stove. The same cooking lesson may not fit both. For the second person, jointly compare labels and affordable ready-to-eat choices, respecting the person’s preferences and medical plan. Ask each learner to demonstrate a relevant decision with a new example. A session can be well delivered yet not remove a transportation barrier; document the barrier and coordinate an appropriate resource rather than treating lack of access as lack of knowledge.

worked_case.scenario: A patient is told to compare sodium on food labels but says, “I am not sure how to use the serving size.” They normally eat two servings from a package. The label shows 350 mg sodium per serving. Design a brief teaching sequence and an evaluation.
worked_case.reasoning: Ask what the patient already looks for and whether they want to work with their usual package. Explain one step at a time: 350 mg per serving × two servings = 700 mg. Use teach-back: “I want to make sure I explained it clearly. How would you calculate the sodium in the amount you normally eat?” If the explanation is incomplete, explain differently and ask again without blame. Give a different label to check transfer of the skill, then agree on a feasible label-comparison action. A later report about using it is a different measure from a skill demonstrated during the visit.

questions.stem: Which objective is most directly observable immediately after a lesson?
options: The patient will understand nutrition forever
Given a sample label, the learner will calculate sodium in two servings
The learner will have perfect health next year
The patient will be motivated in all circumstances
option_rationales: “Understand” alone does not specify a visible performance.
Correct: the task and conditions can be observed and evaluated.
Health outcomes depend on multiple influences and are not an immediate learning performance.
A universal internal state is not directly measurable by this task.

questions.stem: Which question uses teach-back appropriately?
options: Do you understand? Answer yes or no.
I want to check that I explained this clearly. How would you use this label at home?
Repeat my exact words or you have failed.
You understood the handout, correct?
option_rationales: A yes/no response may not reveal whether the explanation was clear.
Correct: the learner explains the action in their own words while the educator owns the clarity of instruction.
Teach-back is not a punitive test of verbatim recall.
This leading yes/no question does not show how the person will use the information.

questions.stem: A label lists 350 mg sodium per serving. A person eats two servings. How much sodium is shown for that amount?
options: 175 mg
350 mg
700 mg
option_rationales: Dividing by two would apply to half a serving, not two.
This is the amount for one serving.
Correct: 350 × 2 = 700 mg.
That is four times the per-serving amount.

questions.stem: Which method best checks a learner’s ability to measure a food portion using a cup?
options: Ask the learner to demonstrate with the cup and provide feedback
Count the number of pamphlets printed
Assume the person can do it if they nod
Measure only the instructor’s speaking time
option_rationales: Correct: observed practice assesses the relevant skill in the stated setting.
A printed-pamphlet count is not a skill assessment.
A nod does not show the procedure.
Speaking time does not establish whether the learner can perform the skill.

questions.stem: A participant correctly describes a plan at the end of education. What can the educator conclude?
options: The participant will certainly follow it indefinitely
The explanation appeared understood at that moment; later behavior and access still need follow-up
The education caused a long-term clinical outcome
There can be no remaining practical barriers
option_rationales: Correct teach-back does not guarantee later action.
Correct: immediate comprehension and later behavior are different outcomes.
A single immediate response does not prove long-term causation.
Practical barriers may remain even when a plan is understood.

questions.stem: A patient cannot shop at the recommended store because they lack transportation. Which response best addresses the stated barrier?
options: Repeat the same handout without discussion
Explore accessible food options and available resources with the patient
Label the patient unmotivated
Set a more demanding shopping goal without asking
option_rationales: The barrier is access, so repeating information alone may not solve it.
Correct: the intervention should respond to the person’s actual barrier and preferences.
The information supplied does not establish motivation.
A goal that ignores the barrier may be impractical.

review: Return to Day 9: identify a modifiable cause before selecting an intervention.
Return to Day 16: explain a cross-contact prevention step using teach-back, then specify how you would assess later use.
Write one objective each for knowledge, demonstrated skill and later behavior; explain how the measures differ.

days.title: Finance and Marketing: Calculate and Decide
objectives: Separate fixed and variable costs, contribution margin and profit in a single-product example.
Calculate a break-even quantity with explicit assumptions and round up when whole units are required.
Use a defined target audience and measurable evidence to evaluate a marketing decision.

theory.heading: 90-minute study session
theory.text: Study this page for 25 minutes, solve the worked case for 15 minutes, answer the questions for 20 minutes, review each explanation and recalculate for 20 minutes, and use 10 minutes for spaced review. Write the formula with units before replacing its symbols. Source links are optional for further study and verification.

theory.heading: Budget, cost behavior and relevant assumptions
theory.text: A budget is a plan for expected revenue and expenses over a stated period. Compare actual amounts with the same budget period and explain a variance before assuming a cause. Fixed costs in a simple model do not change with the number of units within the relevant range and period; variable costs change with units produced or sold. Real operations can contain mixed or step costs and capacity constraints, so label the assumptions used in an exercise. Do not assume every labor cost is fixed or every cost labeled “food” behaves identically. For a single-product problem, the prompt should supply the selling price, variable cost per unit and total fixed costs.

theory.heading: Contribution is not the same as profit
theory.text: Contribution margin per unit equals selling price minus variable cost per unit. It is the amount per unit available to cover fixed costs and, after those are covered under the model, profit. It is not itself net profit. Contribution margin ratio is contribution per unit divided by selling price. If price is $10 and variable cost is $6 per unit, contribution is $4 per unit and the ratio is 40%. At 200 units the total contribution is 200 × $4 = $800. If fixed costs are $600 for that period, modeled profit is $800 − $600 = $200, assuming no omitted costs and that the model’s assumptions hold.

theory.heading: Break-even with whole units
theory.text: For a single product with constant price and variable cost, break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. If fixed costs are $2,500 and contribution is $4 per unit, the mathematical break-even point is 625 units. If fixed costs are $2,501, the quotient is 625.25. When the business can sell only whole units and the question asks for the minimum to avoid a loss, round up to 626 units. At 625 units contribution is $2,500, still $1 short; at 626 it is $2,504. Rounding is determined by the decision and units, not a universal rule for every financial calculation.

theory.heading: Percentages and variance
theory.text: A cost percentage must identify both numerator and denominator. If food cost is $7,200 and food sales are $24,000 in the same period, food cost percentage is $7,200 ÷ $24,000 × 100 = 30%. This does not automatically include labor or establish a net profit margin. If an expense budget was $5,000 and actual expense was $5,400, the expense variance is $400 above budget; the sign and desirability depend on the definition and context. Before recommending a response, check volume, price changes, product mix and whether the underlying figures are comparable. Avoid changing a denominator merely to match a preferred answer.

theory.heading: A target audience is a decision aid
theory.text: Marketing starts with a clearly defined group and a problem the service can address. Describe relevant needs, preferences, location, barriers and competing alternatives; do not assume that everyone who could theoretically use a service will purchase it. Market research can include interviews, surveys or existing data, but each has a sampling limitation. A small survey distributed only to current customers may miss people who do not already use the service. Define what decision the research will inform, ask neutral questions and compare results with other available information. A promotion is a tactic, not proof of demand or program success.

theory.heading: Connect a promotion to a measure
theory.text: Suppose a service tests two different announcements in comparable settings for the same time period. Define the desired action, such as a completed appointment request, and record how many people are reached and how many complete it. If 20 of 200 people reached complete a request, the observed completion proportion is 10% for that defined group. It does not establish that every future audience will respond at the same rate, that all requests lead to sales, or that the announcement alone caused the action. Record the method and limitations; use results to guide a subsequent decision rather than calling raw impressions profit.

theory.heading: Integrated practice: menu choice and pricing
theory.text: A lunch has a price of $12, a variable cost of $7 and fixed period costs of $1,000. Contribution is $5 per lunch; break-even is 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 lunches under the single-product model. At 180 lunches, contribution is $900 and modeled operating result is a $100 loss; at 220 lunches, contribution is $1,100 and modeled result is $100 profit before omitted items. Now imagine raising price to $13 while variable cost remains $7: contribution becomes $6 and mathematical break-even is 166.67, or 167 whole lunches. This does not guarantee that volume stays constant after the price increase; use market evidence and account for capacity before choosing the change.

worked_case.scenario: A clinic meal service is considering one new lunch. The price would be $10, variable cost $6 per lunch, and fixed costs $2,501 per month. The service can sell only whole lunches. A survey of existing customers suggests interest, but employees on evening shifts were not surveyed. What is the minimum modeled break-even volume, and what research question remains?
worked_case.reasoning: Contribution = $10 − $6 = $4 per lunch. Mathematical break-even is $2,501 ÷ $4 = 625.25 lunches, so at least 626 whole lunches are needed to avoid a loss under the stated assumptions. At 625 lunches contribution is $2,500, leaving a $1 shortfall; at 626 it is $2,504. This calculation assumes stable price, variable costs and fixed costs and does not prove demand. Existing customers do not represent the unsurveyed evening group. Ask evening employees about needs, access and likely purchasing behavior before generalizing or choosing a promotion.

questions.stem: A lunch sells for $10 and has $6 in variable cost. What is contribution margin per lunch?
option_rationales: Correct: $10 − $6 = $4 available per unit to cover fixed costs and then profit under the model.
$6 is the variable cost, not the difference.
$10 is sales price before variable cost.
$16 adds the two amounts instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $2,501 per month and contribution is $4 per lunch. If only whole lunches can be sold, what minimum number avoids a loss?
option_rationales: 625 produces $2,500 of contribution, $1 short of fixed costs.
625.25 is the mathematical quotient but not a whole number of lunches.
Correct: round up to 626 whole lunches; contribution is $2,504, or $3 above fixed costs.
This is not the quotient or minimum whole-unit result.

questions.stem: A service reports food costs of $7,200 and food sales of $24,000 for the same period. What is food cost as a percentage of sales?
option_rationales: The decimal is misplaced.
33.3% does not follow from food cost divided by food sales.
70% is the complement, not the food-cost percentage.

questions.stem: An expense budget is $5,000 and the actual expense is $5,400. Which statement is accurate?
options: Expense is $400 above budget
Expense is $400 below budget
Revenue is $400 above budget
The amounts alone prove why costs rose
option_rationales: Correct: actual expense exceeds budget by $400.
The direction is reversed.
The figures concern expense, not revenue.
Further information is needed to explain the variance.

questions.stem: A survey about a new service reaches only existing daytime customers. What should the manager consider before generalizing to evening employees?
options: Evening employees may have different needs and were not represented
The survey automatically includes everyone who could use the service
Existing customers prove future demand at any price
A promotion guarantees that evening employees will enroll
option_rationales: Correct: the sampling frame omits the group in question.
The distribution method explicitly excludes some potential users.
A survey of current customers cannot establish demand at every price.
A tactic does not guarantee a behavioral outcome.

questions.stem: An announcement reaches 200 people and 20 complete the stated appointment-request action. What is the observed request proportion for this group?
option_rationales: Correct: 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%; this does not by itself establish causation or future conversion.
This would be 40 requests out of 200.
This would be 180 requests out of 200.

review: Return to Day 5: explain why contribution margin is not the same as net profit.
Return to Day 17: write units before calculating a rate or percentage, then check the answer by reverse calculation.
Change fixed costs in the worked case to $2,500 and verify that the minimum is exactly 625 lunches; explain the rounding difference.

days.title: Food and Nutrient Science
objectives: Distinguish a food preparation mechanism from a clinical outcome or safety rule.
Use the serving-size basis of a Nutrition Facts label without double-counting added sugars.
Explain how iron form and meal context influence nonheme iron absorption.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes recalling Day 11's association-versus-causation distinction; 25 minutes reading the scientific explanations and sources; 20 minutes working the case and variations; 20 minutes answering and explaining the five questions; and 15 minutes completing the spaced review. Pause to predict an answer before reading each worked step.

theory.heading: Start with the mechanism and the question
theory.text: Food science questions often ask what a preparation step does to structure or texture, whereas nutrition questions ask about composition, intake or physiological use. Identify the outcome before selecting an answer. Heating starch in water allows granules to absorb water and swell, a process called gelatinization that can contribute to thickening. Thickness also depends on the specific starch, formula and method; do not assume that a thickened product has the same properties after every storage or processing condition. Browning and thickening are distinct processes. A change in color or texture alone does not establish that a food reached a safe internal temperature; use the applicable food-safety controls.

theory.heading: Browning, moisture and chemical context
theory.text: The Maillard reaction involves a group of reactions between amino compounds and reducing sugars that can contribute to browning and flavor. Heat, moisture, time and the food's composition influence the result. In a common example, a roasted potato typically develops more brown surface color than a conventionally steamed potato because the wet steaming environment limits surface drying and the familiar dry-heat browning effect. This comparison does not mean that all reactions involving sugars and proteins are chemically impossible in the presence of moisture. Nor is visible browning proof that a food is safe inside. Compare the stated food, surface and method before choosing between similar answers.

theory.heading: Interpret the label per amount actually consumed
theory.text: Nutrition Facts values use the serving size printed on that label, which is not necessarily a recommendation for an individual portion. If the amount consumed differs, multiply the stated per-serving values by servings consumed. 'Includes added sugars' means the listed added sugars are already within total sugars; do not add them a second time. For foods compared on different serving sizes, convert both to a comparable stated amount before comparing nutrients. Percent Daily Value is a reference for a serving, not a personalized prescription, and rounding on a label can produce approximate values. Use food preferences, access and clinical context when applying a label calculation.

theory.heading: Iron form and meal context
theory.text: Heme and nonheme are forms of dietary iron; plant foods and fortified foods provide nonheme iron. Vitamin C-containing foods can enhance the absorption of nonheme iron in a meal. A meal with beans and a vitamin C-rich food is therefore a plausible food-based teaching example. This is a mechanism, not proof that a particular combination alone will correct a person's anemia. A clinician evaluates the cause, laboratory findings, current treatment and relevant interactions. Some components of a meal and a person's overall context also influence absorption, so avoid claiming that one food makes all other considerations irrelevant.

theory.heading: Work a complete label comparison
theory.text: Product A has 160 mg sodium per 40 g serving; Product B has 180 mg sodium per 60 g serving. If the comparison is per 120 g, A supplies 3 servings, or 480 mg, while B supplies 2 servings, or 360 mg. Comparing 160 directly with 180 would favor A per labeled serving but would not answer the equal-weight comparison. Check the units and the actual question before deciding. A lower calculated sodium amount does not by itself settle taste, affordability or all aspects of a person's nutrition plan. Practice: recalculate each product for 80 g—A supplies 320 mg and B supplies 240 mg—and explain the scale factors.

theory.heading: Apply a mechanism without overpromising
theory.text: Suppose a person enjoys lentils and reports difficulty finding fresh vegetables. Ask what fruits or vegetables are affordable and acceptable, including frozen or canned options when appropriate, then explore a vitamin C-containing addition. Explain that the pairing may improve absorption of nonheme iron, while evaluation and prescribed therapy remain important when deficiency is suspected. For the kitchen, distinguish this nutrition goal from a texture goal: a starch slurry can thicken a sauce when heated with liquid, while a dry roasting process can develop browning and different flavors. Describe each process in plain language and check understanding by asking the person to explain how they would adapt a meal. Exercise: write one mechanism, one uncertainty and one practical action; do not convert the mechanism into a guarantee of a laboratory result.

worked_case.scenario: A learner compares a 300 g package containing three 100 g servings. Per serving the label lists 8 g total sugars, including 3 g added sugars, and 240 mg sodium. The learner eats 150 g. A second student claims that adding a vitamin C-rich food to beans always cures iron-deficiency anemia.
worked_case.reasoning: 150 g is 1.5 servings. Total sugars consumed are 8 × 1.5 = 12 g; added sugars are 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 g and are already included in the 12 g. Sodium is 240 × 1.5 = 360 mg. Do not add 12 and 4.5 as if the latter were separate. Vitamin C can enhance nonheme iron absorption, but no single food combination guarantees correction of anemia; the cause and care plan require assessment. Practice: for 200 g calculate 16 g total sugars, 6 g included added sugars and 480 mg sodium. Name one fact supplied by the label and one clinical fact it cannot establish.

questions.stem: A food label lists 90 mg sodium per 30 g serving. How much sodium is listed for 75 g, ignoring label rounding?
options: 150 mg
180 mg
225 mg
270 mg
option_rationales: 150 mg uses fewer than the 2.5 servings consumed.
180 mg is for two servings, or 60 g.
Correct: 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 servings; 90 × 2.5 = 225 mg.
270 mg would describe three 30 g servings.

questions.stem: A label states 10 g total sugars, including 4 g added sugars, per serving. What is the total sugar in one serving?
options: 4 g
6 g
option_rationales: Four grams is the included added-sugars portion, not the full total.
Six grams is the difference, not the labeled total.
Correct: total sugars are 10 g; the 4 g added sugars are already included.
Adding the included portion again double-counts it.

questions.stem: Which meal change can help increase absorption of nonheme iron from beans?
options: Add a vitamin C-rich food to the meal
Assume the iron becomes heme iron
Remove the beans and replace them with water
Claim food pairing alone cures every anemia
option_rationales: Correct: vitamin C can enhance nonheme iron absorption.
The food addition does not convert nonheme iron into heme iron.
Removing the iron-containing food does not achieve the intended pairing.
A mechanism does not establish a cure or replace assessment.

questions.stem: Which process most directly explains a starch-containing sauce becoming thicker when heated with adequate liquid?
options: Starch gelatinization
Protein-to-mineral conversion
Evidence that all microorganisms have died
Guaranteed vitamin retention
option_rationales: Correct: heating starch with water causes swelling that can contribute to thickening.
The stated process does not convert protein into mineral.
Thickness does not prove microbial safety.
The process does not guarantee all vitamins are retained.

questions.stem: Why does a conventionally roasted potato generally develop more brown surface color than a conventionally steamed potato?
options: Dry roasting promotes surface drying and conditions favorable to browning
Steam makes all chemical reactions impossible
Browning proves the potato has no moisture
Brown color independently establishes a safe internal temperature
option_rationales: Correct: the comparison depends on heat, surface moisture, time and composition.
The existence of moisture does not make all reactions impossible.
A browned food can still contain moisture.
Color is not a substitute for appropriate food-safety controls.

review: Explain the difference between starch gelatinization and Maillard browning without notes.
Convert Product B in the example to 180 g: three 60 g servings provide 540 mg sodium; explain why equivalent amounts are necessary for comparison.
Recall Day 11: state why a plausible absorption mechanism does not itself prove a clinical outcome in every person.

days.title: Ethics, Practice, and Compliance
objectives: Distinguish professional competence, organizational policy and applicable law in a practice decision.
Apply the HIPAA minimum-necessary concept to the purpose stated in a scenario, recognizing treatment exceptions.
Document relevant facts objectively and respond to a potential conflict of interest.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes recalling Day 12's assessment-to-action sequence; 25 minutes reading the sections and sources; 20 minutes working the confidentiality case and its variations; 20 minutes answering questions and explaining each option; and 15 minutes on the spaced-review prompts. The scenarios are educational; actual legal decisions require the applicable facts, law and organizational procedures.

theory.heading: Start with the role and the purpose
theory.text: Professional standards, facility policy and law answer related but different questions. Professional ethics informs duties such as competence and integrity. Scope and competence help determine whether a practitioner is prepared and authorized to perform a task. An organization's policy may define workflows and reporting, while federal, state and local law can impose separate requirements. A credential alone does not settle every state-specific permission or prove competence in every specialty. When a question omits the location or practice setting, do not invent an absolute legal conclusion. Identify the immediate patient need, the practitioner's current competence and the relevant policy or source to consult.

theory.heading: Competence and referral
theory.text: The nutrition and dietetics Code of Ethics calls for evidence-based practice within areas of competence and continued professional development. If asked to provide an intervention beyond current competence, acknowledge the limitation; seek appropriate supervision, education or referral according to policy and the patient's needs. Do not abandon an urgent concern while waiting for an ideal specialist. Escalate as appropriate, document what is known and arrange a safe next step. Contrast an unfamiliar but trainable task with a practitioner asserting expertise they do not have. In an exam vignette, choose the action that protects the client and obtains appropriate help rather than the answer that conceals uncertainty.

theory.heading: Privacy: identify the disclosure
theory.text: For a HIPAA-covered entity, the minimum-necessary standard generally requires reasonable efforts to limit certain uses, disclosures and requests for protected health information to what is needed for the intended purpose. HHS identifies exceptions, including disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment and disclosures to the individual who is the subject of the information. Do not apply a simplistic rule that every treatment disclosure is subject to the same minimum-necessary restriction, and do not infer that an exception eliminates other privacy and security responsibilities. Role-based access, organizational policies, appropriate safeguards and the reason for access still matter. State the recipient and purpose before applying a rule.

theory.heading: Separate payment, treatment and authorization
theory.text: Suppose a staff member requests information for a routine payment function at a covered entity. The organization generally uses appropriate minimum-necessary policies for that purpose; it need not send the entire record merely because it is convenient. In contrast, HHS explains that the minimum-necessary standard does not apply to disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment. Each scenario still calls for appropriate verification, safeguards and applicable policy. A permitted disclosure for an identified purpose is not the same as permission to browse records out of curiosity. Patient-specific restrictions, other laws and the actual organizational context may also matter; the exercise does not decide every disclosure question.

theory.heading: Objective documentation and correction
theory.text: Document observations, sources of information, clinical reasoning and actions in accordance with the organization's record policy. Separate a reported statement from a measured finding: 'patient reports eating one meal yesterday' is different from 'all meals are refused.' Include the date or time where material, identify uncertainties and record the planned follow-up. If an entry is incorrect, follow the organization's approved correction procedure so the correction is traceable; do not conceal the original or fabricate a result. When handing off an unresolved issue, state what remains unknown, who will act and what circumstances require escalation.

theory.heading: Conflicts, consent and difficult choices
theory.text: A conflict of interest may arise when a recommendation could benefit the practitioner financially. Identify the relationship, follow relevant disclosure and institutional policies, and base advice on the person's needs and evidence. Do not imply that disclosure alone automatically makes every arrangement permissible. Respect the person's choices and explain the benefits, limitations and alternatives within your role; an informed discussion should be understandable to the person. If a concern involves immediate safety, escalate through the appropriate team channel. Exercise: write one sentence describing the clinical decision, one describing the potential personal interest and one describing the next policy or supervisory step.

worked_case.scenario: An RDN working for a covered hospital is asked by a billing employee to send an entire nutrition record for a routine payment task even though the employee identifies only two fields as needed. Later, another treating clinician asks for information needed for a current treatment decision. A vendor has also offered the RDN a personal payment to recommend a product.
worked_case.reasoning: For the payment request, follow organizational policy and generally apply the minimum-necessary principle to the stated purpose; verify the recipient and relevant fields rather than sending the whole record for convenience. HHS identifies an exception to that standard for disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment; this is not permission for unrelated access and other safeguards still apply. The payment offer creates a potential conflict: follow disclosure and organizational policies, use evidence and client needs, and do not imply a personal benefit determines the recommendation. Practice: rewrite the first request as a direct request from the patient for their own record and identify why the minimum-necessary analysis changes.

questions.stem: An RDN is asked to perform a specialty procedure outside their current competence. Which response best fits ethical practice?
options: Conceal the limitation and proceed independently
Seek appropriate supervision, training or referral while ensuring a safe next step
Refuse to communicate any patient concern
Advertise expertise before obtaining it
option_rationales: Concealing limitations risks unsafe care and undermines integrity.
Correct: recognize limits and obtain appropriate support while addressing the person's needs.
A concern may still require communication and escalation.
A credential or advertisement does not establish competence in every procedure.

questions.stem: For a routine payment disclosure by a HIPAA-covered entity, which approach generally follows HHS minimum-necessary guidance?
options: Disclose only information reasonably needed for the identified purpose under policy
Send every record because billing is always exempt
Disclose to any recipient who asks
Assume HIPAA bans every payment disclosure
option_rationales: Correct: the standard generally limits applicable uses, disclosures and requests to what is reasonably needed.
Payment is not the treatment-provider exception described in the source.
Recipient and purpose must be verified; a request alone is not enough.
HIPAA permits applicable disclosures under its rules; this absolute ban is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which disclosure is explicitly excepted from HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard according to HHS?
options: A disclosure to a health care provider for treatment
Every disclosure made for marketing
A disclosure to any coworker out of curiosity
Every disclosure to an unidentified vendor
option_rationales: Correct: HHS identifies disclosures to or requests by a provider for treatment as an exception.
An advertising purpose is not the stated treatment exception.
Curiosity is not an identified treatment disclosure.
An unidentified recipient and unspecified purpose do not establish the exception.

questions.stem: An RDN receives a personal incentive to recommend a supplement. What is the best next step?
options: Follow conflict-of-interest policies and base advice on evidence and client needs
Recommend it to everyone without disclosure
Assume disclosure automatically makes any arrangement permissible
Hide the relationship if the product is available over the counter
option_rationales: Correct: identify the potential conflict and follow applicable policy while centering client needs.
Universal recommendations for personal gain neglect the client's needs and the conflict.
Disclosure is relevant but does not independently establish every arrangement is permissible.
Availability without prescription does not remove the conflict.

questions.stem: A patient reports eating one meal yesterday, but intake was not directly observed. Which documentation is most precise?
options: Patient reports eating one meal yesterday
Patient definitely ate exactly one meal, directly observed
Patient never eats more than one meal
No nutrition information was obtained
option_rationales: Correct: it identifies the source and scope of the information.
The scenario says the intake was not directly observed.
One reported day cannot establish a permanent pattern.
A relevant reported intake history was obtained.

review: Explain in your own words the HIPAA treatment-provider exception and one safeguard that can remain relevant.
Revisit Day 19: distinguish a purchasing policy from a binding legal requirement in a particular jurisdiction.
Write a two-sentence objective note identifying one fact observed, one patient-reported fact and a next step.

days.title: Integrated Cases and Remaining Gaps
objectives: Use a consistent decision sequence when a case mixes assessment, calculations, management and safety.
Identify when missing data or an unverified assumption prevents a confident decision.
Apply formulas and rules to new values, then review the reason each distractor is less suitable.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes selecting one pending topic from your checklist; 20 minutes reviewing the decision framework below; 20 minutes working the integrated case and its variations; 25 minutes answering and reviewing the original case questions; and 15 minutes recording corrections and next steps. If you have time later, use the app's domain practice for additional reviewed questions. The five new questions here are a focused case set, not a 25–35-question simulated exam.

theory.heading: A five-step framework
theory.text: First identify the decision the prompt actually asks for: screen, assess, diagnose, intervene, monitor or manage a production step. Second, list facts supplied and avoid filling gaps with an assumed diagnosis or unstated schedule. Third, check urgent safety concerns and the appropriate professional role. Fourth, compare the plausible options against the decisive evidence and the applicable source or stated assumption. Fifth, choose a measurable follow-up and explain what new information would change the decision. A number may be correct arithmetic yet be an inappropriate clinical prescription; a plausible intervention may address the wrong cause.

theory.heading: Clinical information in context
theory.text: In a patient with reduced intake, obtain the timing, amount, barriers, weights and relevant physical findings. A positive screen indicates risk and supports further assessment, but does not by itself establish a severity diagnosis. During an acute illness, serum albumin can reflect inflammation and is not alone an accepted diagnostic measure of malnutrition. If the recorded weights were measured under different conditions, verify the trend before relying on it. Ask what data are missing, and distinguish an urgent action from a longer-term plan. When an intervention is selected, monitor a measure that matches the goal, such as intake and tolerance for an intake intervention.

theory.heading: Carry units through a production calculation
theory.text: Consider an order requiring a specified edible portion. First compute usable quantity in the same unit as the yield. Divide EP by the supplied AP-to-EP yield fraction, check the answer by multiplication, then account for usable stock in AP units. Only after the shortfall is known should you round up to the available whole package size. A yield for a different product or preparation is not interchangeable. To compare two per-serving nutrition labels, first convert them to the same quantity. Write the unit after each operation; this prevents treating ounces of volume as ounces of weight.

theory.heading: Timing, hazards and documentation
theory.text: When a food-safety case names FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14 for cooling cooked TCS food, check both 135°F to 70°F within two hours and 135°F to 41°F or below within six hours total. A rapid first stage does not extend the six-hour total. A missed limit requires action under the applicable plan and local requirements; later temperature or smell alone does not erase the documented deviation. In an ethics case, identify the intended recipient and purpose of a disclosure before applying the relevant rule. Document the facts, the decision and the follow-up objectively.

theory.heading: Compare the two most tempting alternatives
theory.text: For each question, write a short justification for the leading option and a separate reason the nearest alternative fails. For instance, a person with new edema and reduced intake may have a stable scale weight; 'no change in nutrition status' ignores the possibility of fluid masking weight changes, while 'exactly 5 kg of tissue loss' invents a value not supplied. The useful next step is to gather and verify additional findings. A correct answer should follow from the scenario rather than from an absolute word such as always or never. Avoid choosing an answer merely because it resembles a memorized previous case.

theory.heading: Turn an error into a transfer task
theory.text: Classify the cause of an error tentatively: unfamiliar content, arithmetic or units, misread timing, ignored qualifier, or excessive time spent between similar alternatives. Then change one fact and solve again. If a 10 lb EP requirement at 80% yield becomes 12 lb, recalculate: 12 ÷ 0.80 = 15 lb AP before stock. If the number of whole bags is requested, state bag size before rounding. If a fact or source remains disputed, mark the item for review rather than scoring a guessed key as certainty. This deliberate correction is part of study time, not an optional step after counting questions.

worked_case.scenario: A foodservice operation will serve 80 portions requiring 2.4 oz each of a specified ready-to-serve vegetable. Verified yield is 75% from AP to that form. The operation has 3 lb AP of safe, uncommitted stock and buys whole 5 lb bags. During the same shift, a patient reports decreased intake and new edema; a low albumin value is recorded during inflammation. A soup log shows 70°F at 90 minutes and 41°F at 5 hours total.
worked_case.reasoning: Vegetable EP = 80 × 2.4 oz = 192 oz = 12 lb. Required AP = 12 ÷ 0.75 = 16 lb; after 3 lb stock, order at least 13 lb. Three 5 lb bags are needed. Verify the yield and stock assumptions. For the patient, obtain intake and weight histories and relevant findings; edema can mask weight change, and low albumin alone is not a malnutrition diagnosis. The soup meets the two stated FDA 2026 cooling time limits, assuming valid readings and applicable conditions. These are three different decisions; document and follow up separately. Variation: with only 1 lb usable stock, the AP shortfall is 15 lb, still three bags.

questions.stem: A menu requires 18 lb usable produce. Yield to the specified form is 75%, and 4 lb AP of uncommitted stock is available. How much additional AP is needed before package rounding?
options: 20 lb
22 lb
24 lb
option_rationales: 13.5 lb multiplies EP by yield, rather than dividing to find AP.
The given yield and stock do not produce 22 lb.
24 lb is the total AP requirement before subtracting stock.

questions.stem: A patient has low albumin during inflammation and new edema, but no reliable intake history. What is the best next step?
options: Diagnose severe malnutrition from albumin alone
Collect and verify intake, weight and other relevant assessment findings
Assume stable scale weight rules out tissue loss
Delay all assessment until inflammation resolves
option_rationales: Albumin alone is not an accepted stand-alone malnutrition diagnostic measure.
Correct: obtain a comprehensive assessment and account for fluid context.
Edema may obscure weight change.
Inflammation does not eliminate the need to assess.

questions.stem: For a covered entity's disclosure to a health care provider for treatment, which statement reflects HHS guidance?
options: The HIPAA minimum-necessary standard does not apply to that disclosure; other safeguards can still matter
All disclosures to any recipient for any purpose are exempt
The entire record may be accessed for curiosity
Every disclosure for treatment is prohibited
option_rationales: Correct: HHS identifies the provider-treatment exception, while other rules and safeguards remain relevant.
The exception is not a general exemption for all purposes.
Curiosity is not an authorized treatment purpose.
HIPAA does not prohibit every treatment disclosure.

questions.stem: Under FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14, cooked TCS food reaches 70°F at 1 hour and 41°F at 6 hours 10 minutes total. Which condition was missed?
options: The first-stage two-hour limit
The six-hour total cooling limit
Neither limit
The record proves a specific pathogen is present
option_rationales: The first stage is within two hours.
Correct: the final temperature was reached ten minutes after the six-hour total.
The final total is outside the stated limit.
A time-temperature deviation does not identify a specific pathogen.

questions.stem: A learner chooses the right answer after remembering its letter from a prior attempt. What best checks transferable understanding?
options: Change a key fact and explain the reasoning for each option
Assume the learner has mastered the full domain
Repeat the same option order until faster
Ignore the underlying reason
option_rationales: Correct: a new variation and option-by-option reasoning test the concept more directly.
One recognized answer does not establish mastery.
The same order can reinforce recognition rather than transfer.
The reasoning is central to identifying and correcting the knowledge gap.

review: Return to Day 13 and classify one decision as an observed fact, an inference or an assumption.
Rework the case with a new yield and package size, documenting each unit and rounding only the final package count.
List gaps as not yet covered, practiced with support, or applied correctly to a new case; use the plan to select a concrete next action.

days.title: Light Review and Adjustment
objectives: Retrieve key concepts from the recent study block and apply them to changed facts.
Separate incomplete coverage from a demonstrated recurring difficulty.
Choose next steps based on source quality, exam-domain importance and actual evidence rather than a pass prediction.

theory.heading: Suggested 45-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 8 minutes retrieving one principle each from food science, ethics, management and clinical assessment; 12 minutes on the worked case and its changed-value variation; 15 minutes answering the four questions and reviewing explanations; and 10 minutes updating the topic checklist. Keep the session light rather than adding new topics to make up for an earlier delay.

theory.heading: Review across contexts
theory.text: A correct calculation requires a stated unit and denominator. A food label's total sugars already include listed added sugars. A purchase calculation converts the required edible portion into an as-purchased amount by dividing by the applicable yield. A nutrition assessment uses multiple verified findings; inflammation can affect albumin and fluid can affect scale weight. For professional practice, identify the role, recipient and disclosure purpose before selecting a privacy rule. These principles interact in real cases, but one correct answer in each does not demonstrate complete domain mastery.

theory.heading: Make a precise adjustment
theory.text: Mark a topic as not yet studied, studied with support, or applied correctly to a fresh case. When an answer was wrong or guessed, describe the cause as a hypothesis: missing knowledge, calculation, reading a qualifier, or time pressure. Choose no more than two priority gaps for the next block, considering the 2026 outline's domain emphasis and actual study evidence. Do not treat 2026 weights as the 2027 outline; confirm the applicable official outline for the eventual exam. A short authored set is not a calibrated score and does not predict a pass.

worked_case.scenario: A product lists 12 g total sugars including 5 g added sugars per 50 g serving. A person eats 75 g. Separately, a patient has low albumin during inflammation but no documented intake history. The learner has not yet studied renal nutrition and guessed a food-safety answer.
worked_case.reasoning: The portion is 1.5 servings. Total sugars are 18 g; the 7.5 g added sugars are included in that total. For the patient, collect intake and other relevant assessment information rather than diagnosing malnutrition from albumin alone. Mark renal nutrition as not yet studied, not automatically weak. Revisit the guessed safety item, check its cited source, then test the rule with changed times. These observations guide study but cannot predict an exam result. Variation: at 100 g the portion is two servings, or 24 g total sugars including 10 g added sugars.

questions.stem: A package lists 14 g total sugars including 6 g added sugars per serving. How much total sugar is in two servings?
option_rationales: 12 g is the added-sugar amount in two servings, not total sugars.
16 g is not the total for two stated servings.
Correct: 14 × 2 = 28 g total; included added sugars are 12 g.
Adding the included added sugars again double-counts them.

questions.stem: A positive nutrition-risk screen identifies a patient who may be at risk. What should it prompt?
options: A comprehensive nutrition assessment when appropriate
A severe-malnutrition diagnosis without further evidence
No action until an albumin result is available
The same prescription for every patient
option_rationales: Correct: the screen helps identify the need for further assessment.
Screening does not alone establish severity.
A nutrition assessment need not wait for albumin to fall.
A plan must reflect the individual's context.

questions.stem: A learner has not yet reviewed a topic and scores well on four questions from other areas. How should the topic be classified?
options: Not yet studied
Mastered based on unrelated questions
Definitely a persistent weakness
Covered because the title appears on the plan
option_rationales: Correct: its study status is not yet studied.
Results on other areas do not establish mastery of this topic.
Lack of exposure is not proof of recurring difficulty.
A topic title is not evidence of completed study.

questions.stem: A provider requests patient information from another health care provider for treatment. According to HHS, which statement about HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard is accurate?
options: It does not apply to that provider-to-provider treatment disclosure
It automatically prohibits the disclosure
It applies identically to every possible request without exception
It allows unrelated curiosity-driven access
option_rationales: Correct: HHS identifies treatment-provider disclosures as an exception to that standard.
The cited standard does not automatically prohibit this treatment disclosure.
HHS lists exceptions, including the treatment-provider case.
A stated exception does not justify unrelated access.

review: Write the two top study priorities only after identifying what was actually covered and which uncertainties persist.
Choose one guessed item, check the primary source and solve a changed-value version before counting it as understood.
Record that this light review is not an official score or pass prediction.

days.title: Priority Gap A: Choose, Explain, and Test
objectives: Choose a provisional first remediation topic using actual evidence or a transparent fallback, not an assumed weakness.
Distinguish a concept gap from reading, vocabulary, calculation, time or source uncertainty.
Apply retrieval and a new case to check reasoning without treating a small sample as a pass prediction.

theory.heading: A 90-minute study session
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes choosing a topic using the method below, 25 minutes studying and recalling the relevant content, 15 minutes on the worked case, 20 minutes answering the questions, 15 minutes reviewing every option and recording reasons, and five minutes planning a spaced revisit. All core explanations and examples are on this page; the sources are optional for further verification. Use an accessible topic rather than waiting for a perfect analysis.

theory.heading: Start with evidence, not a label
theory.text: This lesson does not know your current history or identify your weaknesses. If you have a recent, trustworthy record, list topic, number of new questions, incorrect answers, guesses and an explanation of what went wrong. Include material you have not yet studied; zero attempts means coverage is unknown, not strong or weak. A single wrong answer can reflect a misread or a lucky-looking distractor and is not enough to rank an entire domain. If records are missing, choose a subtopic that has not yet been studied or use the example below. Label it a starting point rather than a diagnosis of your ability.

theory.heading: Use the applicable content outline
theory.text: For the CDR outline effective January 1, 2022 through December 31, 2026, the stated domain weights are I 21%, II 45%, III 21% and IV 13%. These weights concern exam content distribution, not a personal score, the number of hours you must spend, or proof that one missed question is more important. Before an exam in 2027 or later, check the outline that applies to that exam date; do not carry 2026 weights forward automatically. Within the applicable outline, prefer an unstudied or repeatedly difficult important subtopic, but maintain some review of the other domains. Do not infer the candidate’s scheduled date.

theory.heading: Classify the reason before deciding the remedy
theory.text: Knowledge: the principle was unavailable even after careful reading. Interpretation: a word such as minimum, except, first, or per serving was missed. Calculation: the setup, unit conversion or arithmetic failed. Time: the explanation was known afterward but the decision took too long; investigate the cause rather than assuming every slow answer is a knowledge deficit. Vocabulary: a term blocked understanding; define it in English and use it in a new sentence. Source uncertainty: two reputable references or editions appear inconsistent; keep the item unresolved while checking scope and date. A single answer can have more than one contributing reason.

theory.heading: A repeatable remediation cycle
theory.text: First write the decision rule from memory, leaving blanks for what you cannot recall. Then study the explanation and a suitable source; identify the condition under which the rule applies. Work one example, explain why each plausible alternative is wrong or less appropriate, and solve a new variation with one relevant fact changed. Record the original condition, the decision and the new result. Revisit after an interval using retrieval before looking. The IES practice guide recommends spacing learning and using tests to promote learning; this is a study strategy, not proof of a particular exam score.

theory.heading: Illustration, not your own results
theory.text: Imagine a learner completed ten new questions in clinical calculations and missed four, but also guessed two of the six correct answers. The learner discovers that three misses involved units, while the fourth concerned a clinical fact not yet checked. A reasonable provisional activity is to practice writing units and inverse checks, while separately verifying the disputed fact. It would be premature to assert that the learner will fail the clinical domain or to compare 6/10 with an official passing standard. The numbers in this illustration are invented for instruction and do not describe your history.

theory.heading: Worked calculation: prescribed target versus universal recommendation
theory.text: A case states that a clinician has chosen a protein target of 0.8 g/kg/day for a particular 65-kg adult. The arithmetic is 65 × 0.8 = 52 g/day. The phrase “chosen for this case” matters: the computation does not make 0.8 g/kg a universal target for all people with kidney disease or every treatment. To test transfer, change weight to 75 kg while keeping the supplied target unchanged: 75 × 0.8 = 60 g/day. Then change the question: if no target is supplied, the correct response is not to invent one; gather patient-specific data and coordinate with the clinical team.

theory.heading: Make the next check useful
theory.text: A comparison is more informative when you know the source, topic, number of items and conditions, and when you test with new or revised questions instead of repeatedly recognizing the same letter. Keep the denominator visible: 3 correct out of 4 is 75%, but four items give limited information about a broad domain. If one new variation succeeds, describe that specific success; do not claim the entire topic is mastered. For a persistent difficulty, make the action smaller: define one term, set up one calculation or identify the decision step. Note the source and schedule another recall attempt.

theory.heading: Applied selection practice with a model answer
theory.text: Suppose a learner has no dependable recent scores and has not reviewed nutrition assessment or foodservice production. They choose nutrition assessment for today because it is unstudied and is part of Domain II in the 2026 outline; they record foodservice for a later session. A suitable objective is “identify which missing intake information is needed before a nutrition intervention,” followed by a new scenario. Another learner could reasonably choose foodservice first based on its own evidence or constraints. Neither choice proves a personal weakness. Return to the other domain in spaced review so that choosing a priority does not become permanent neglect.

worked_case.scenario: A hypothetical student has no reliable current results. They have not reviewed clinical calculations and have only read about food production. The 2026 outline is applicable to this example. They decide to begin with clinical calculations. The next case provides a formula concentration of 1.25 kcal/mL and an ordered energy amount of 1,500 kcal. How should they study and check the decision?
worked_case.reasoning: Label the choice provisional and based on coverage, not an inferred weakness. Set up volume = prescribed kcal ÷ kcal/mL: 1,500 ÷ 1.25 = 1,200 mL. Reverse-check 1,200 × 1.25 = 1,500 kcal. Explain why the concentration is a divisor and why the given energy amount is an order in this exercise, not a universal prescription. Try a new concentration or delivery schedule, classify any error, and schedule food production for later review. One successful calculation is evidence about that task, not a prediction of the exam score.

questions.stem: A learner has no trustworthy current performance data. What is a defensible way to choose today’s first review topic?
options: Declare the highest-weight domain the learner’s confirmed weakness
Choose an unstudied topic provisionally and record that the choice is based on coverage
Treat zero attempts as evidence of mastery
Predict an exam score from the absence of data
option_rationales: A content weight does not reveal an individual weakness.
Correct: coverage is a transparent fallback, and the conclusion remains provisional.
No attempts provide no direct evidence of mastery.
An absent sample cannot support a score prediction.

questions.stem: A learner knows the relevant formula but uses the per-serving value without multiplying by two servings. Which review category is most directly supported?
options: A reading or interpretation error concerning the stated amount
Proof that all nutrition science knowledge is absent
A confirmed long-term time-management disorder
A source conflict that must be resolved by changing a guideline
option_rationales: Correct: the stated amount was overlooked in applying the known rule.
One error does not support this sweeping conclusion.
No timing or diagnostic evidence is provided.
The problem gives no conflicting source or guideline.

questions.stem: A clinical team supplies a case-specific protein target of 0.8 g/kg/day for a 65-kg adult. What is the calculated amount?
options: 52 g/day
65.8 g/day
81.25 g/day
520 g/day
option_rationales: Correct: 65 × 0.8 = 52 g/day; the target is specified for this case.
Adding the numbers does not apply the target.
Division gives a different result and unit relationship.
This is a tenfold decimal error.

questions.stem: Which practice best checks transfer after reviewing a calculation?
options: Repeat the same answer letter until it feels familiar
Solve a new scenario with a changed value and explain the setup
Delete the original problem and avoid all variations
Assume one correct response proves complete mastery
option_rationales: Letter familiarity is not evidence that the method transfers.
Correct: a variation tests the rule and its conditions.
Avoiding variation does not test transfer.
One item supports only a limited conclusion.

questions.stem: A learner gets 3 correct on 4 new questions in a subtopic. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: A 75% sample proves official exam readiness
The observed result is 75%, but four questions are limited evidence about the broader topic
The learner missed 75%
The observed percentage is the official scaled score
option_rationales: Four items cannot establish official readiness.
Correct: 3 ÷ 4 = 75%, with a small denominator and limited scope.
One of four was missed, which is 25%.
A practice percentage is not the official scaled score.

questions.stem: Two reputable sources appear to give different recommendations. Which first response supports safe review?
options: Select the one with the larger number without reading it
Check the population, date, edition and context before resolving the difference
Average the recommendations automatically
Mark both sources wrong without checking
option_rationales: The larger number alone does not establish applicability.
Correct: apparent disagreement may reflect different populations, versions or conditions.
Averaging may produce a recommendation supported by neither source.
The information is insufficient to reject both.

review: Return to Day 15: compare an arithmetic prescription supplied for a case with a general recommendation.
Return to Day 22: identify one limitation when a small group is treated as representative of a larger population.
Write one provisional priority and the actual reason for choosing it; if no personal record exists, write “coverage unknown.”

days.title: Priority Gap B: Contrast Decisions and Distractors
objectives: Choose a second provisional study priority without assuming personal strengths or weaknesses.
Compare a correct action with a plausible alternative using the facts and conditions of the case.
Distinguish implementation, measurement and causal interpretation in management and education cases.

theory.heading: A 90-minute study session
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes choosing a second topic, 25 minutes studying the concepts below or your chosen material, 15 minutes on the worked case, 20 minutes on questions, 15 minutes explaining each option, and five minutes setting the next review. The examples here are instructional and are not a description of your own results. Linked sources provide optional verification, not a required separate reading assignment.

theory.heading: Select priority B without inventing a profile
theory.text: If you have dependable evidence, choose a second subtopic using its coverage, recurring reasoning issue, relevance to the applicable exam outline and available study time. If not, choose a topic you have not yet studied or use this management and education example. Do not assign yourself a weak-domain label based on one item or the absence of records. Priority B can be in the same domain as A if the evidence supports that choice, but include other domains in periodic mixed review. Record the reason for selection and what result would justify revisiting the decision.

theory.heading: Compare the decision, not just the topic name
theory.text: Before looking at options, identify the task: assessment, intervention, monitoring, management calculation or evaluation. Then ask what information in the stem changes the decision. Several options may be generally useful but only one may directly answer the specified question. The goal is to explain why the selected option fits this case and why each alternative does not. Avoid adding missing facts to make a favorite answer work. If two options remain equally defensible under the stated assumptions, identify the ambiguity rather than memorizing the key.

theory.heading: Management example: measures and actions
theory.text: A team distributes 200 invitations to a cooking class, holds two classes and enrolls 30 people. These figures describe activities or direct outputs. They do not establish that participants later changed a meal, improved food access or achieved a health outcome. If the objective is that participants use a particular local resource within four weeks, a follow-up measure should ask about that use with a clear numerator, denominator and time. In a logic model, staff time and funding are inputs, holding the class is an activity, classes held or participants reached are outputs, and changes in access or behavior are potential outcomes. Each type answers a different question.

theory.heading: Education example: teach-back versus attendance
theory.text: An educator demonstrates how to use a nutrition label. Asking “How would you use this information for the amount you normally eat?” invites the learner to explain in their own words and checks the clarity of the explanation. If the explanation is unclear, the educator can rephrase and ask again without blame. Counting handouts does not measure that skill. A correct teach-back at the visit indicates understanding at that time; it does not prove that the person later changed behavior or had access to the proposed food. Follow-up should match the stated objective and consider practical barriers.

theory.heading: A financial contrast with explicit assumptions
theory.text: For one product, suppose sales price is $12 per lunch, variable cost is $7 per lunch and fixed costs are $1,000 for the month. Contribution per lunch is $5, so the break-even calculation is $1,000 ÷ $5 = 200 lunches under the stated single-product assumptions. At 180 lunches, total contribution is $900, leaving a $100 modeled shortfall before omitted costs. Do not call the $5 contribution “net profit” or divide by sales price alone. If the question asks for whole units and the quotient is fractional, use the smallest integer that covers fixed costs. Real services can have multiple products, price changes and capacity constraints.

theory.heading: Separate association from proof
theory.text: Suppose a program’s reported meal planning rises after an education class. The change can motivate further investigation, but other events or participant differences may contribute. The strength of a causal conclusion depends on the evaluation design, comparison and evidence. Consider who did not respond and whether the measure is the same at both times. A higher count of distributed leaflets cannot substitute for a measure of the stated participant outcome. When an answer claims that one intervention “proved” a result with only a before-and-after observation, inspect the assumptions and limitations.

theory.heading: A method for the closest distractor
theory.text: After selecting an answer, name the attractive distractor and the fact that makes it less suitable. Example: if the objective is to determine whether a learner can measure a portion, counting attendance is tempting because it is easy to collect, but it measures reach rather than performance of the skill. Ask the learner to demonstrate with a measuring cup and observe the steps. Now change the objective to whether the person used the method at home: a later follow-up question becomes relevant, although it remains self-report. This contrast practices transfer instead of memorizing a fixed answer.

theory.heading: Track uncertainty and progress fairly
theory.text: A short study log can hold the topic, item source, decision rule, reason for an error or guess, a new variation and date of the next review. Keep facts separate from interpretations: “I missed two calculations because I divided by the sales price” is an observation about specific items; “I cannot do finance” is an unsupported global label. If a source is ambiguous, retain the question for review rather than changing a key by intuition. A later correct answer on a new item is useful feedback, but a small sample remains limited. Explain the concepts in English using ordinary professional terms.

worked_case.scenario: A service wants to know whether a label-reading lesson improved participants’ ability to calculate sodium for their usual portion. It printed 100 handouts, taught 20 people and later observed 12 people solve a new label example correctly. What does each number show, and what additional information matters?
worked_case.reasoning: Handouts printed and people taught are direct implementation or reach measures. The 12 correct demonstrations measure the stated skill only for those assessed, using the specific new example. The denominator and missing observations must be stated: if all 20 were assessed, 12/20 = 60%; if only 12 were assessed and all 12 were correct, the observed assessed-group result is 12/12, not 12/20. Neither figure alone proves later behavior, clinical impact or causation. Ask which participants were assessed, how the task was scored and what follow-up decision the team needs.

questions.stem: A program prints 100 handouts and wants to know whether participants can calculate a label amount. Which measure most directly matches that objective?
options: Count only the printed handouts
Ask learners to calculate an amount from a new sample label
Count the program’s email addresses
Assume attendance proves the calculation skill
option_rationales: Handouts printed is an output, not a direct skill measure.
Correct: a new calculation demonstrates the stated skill under the conditions of the assessment.
The number of email addresses does not measure calculation ability.
Attendance and skill performance are different measures.

questions.stem: A lunch sells for $12; its variable cost is $7. Monthly fixed costs are $1,000. Under a single-product model, what number of lunches gives exact break-even?
option_rationales: 100 lunches yield $500 contribution, below fixed costs.
143 lunches yield $715 contribution.
Correct: contribution is $5; $1,000 ÷ $5 = 200.
This incorrectly uses the fixed-cost amount as the unit count.

questions.stem: After an educator explains a label, which statement is teach-back?
options: Did you understand?
I want to check my explanation. How would you use the serving size for your usual amount?
Repeat my words exactly to pass the test.
You will use this correctly every time, right?
option_rationales: A yes/no response may not show what was understood.
Correct: the learner explains the action in their own words, and the educator checks clarity.
Teach-back is not a punitive verbatim test.
A leading prediction does not demonstrate current understanding.

questions.stem: Twenty people attend a class, and all 20 are assessed with a new task; 12 answer it correctly. What proportion of this assessed group answered correctly?
option_rationales: 12 is the count, not the percentage.
40% would be 8 out of 20.
80% would be 16 out of 20.

questions.stem: A learner can justify two options equally well because a stem omits a key condition. What is the best response during review?
options: Invent the missing condition to force a preferred answer
Mark the issue as ambiguous and check the source or clarify the stem
Assume both options are always correct in every context
Ignore the discrepancy because the answer key exists
option_rationales: Adding unsupported facts can hide the problem.
Correct: a missing condition should be adjudicated rather than guessed.
The ambiguity does not establish a universal rule.
A key alone does not resolve an under-specified question.

questions.stem: A program records higher self-reported meal planning after a class, without a comparison group. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The class alone definitively caused the change
A change was observed, but alternative explanations and the evaluation design matter
The program has no need to review missing responses
Attendance is exactly the same as the later behavior
option_rationales: An uncontrolled observation does not establish this causal claim.
Correct: describe the observation and consider limitations before inferring causation.
Missing responses may affect interpretation.
Reach and later behavior are different measures.

review: Return to Day 23: write one knowledge objective and one observed-skill measure.
Return to Day 24: recalculate the lunch example if fixed costs are $1,001; 201 whole lunches are needed to avoid a modeled loss.
Return to Day 29: identify whether one missed example reflects content, interpretation, arithmetic, time or uncertainty; multiple causes are possible.

days.title: Mixed Practice and Transfer: Change One Fact
objectives: Apply a decision rule to a new case with a relevant condition changed.
Move among clinical, education, management and foodservice questions without losing units or context.
Record the reason for an answer and the limits of evidence, then plan a spaced retest.

theory.heading: A 90-minute study session
theory.text: Spend 20 minutes reviewing the examples on this page, 15 minutes on the worked case, 25 minutes answering mixed questions, 20 minutes explaining why each option fits or does not fit, and 10 minutes on spaced review. All examples are hypothetical. This exercise does not use or infer personal results; apply it to your own records only if those are available and reliable. Source links are optional for further verification.

theory.heading: Transfer is more than recognition
theory.text: A rule is useful when you can identify when it applies, use it with changed values and explain when it would not apply. First recall the rule without looking; next read the new case and mark the requested output, relevant units and limiting words. Change one fact at a time and predict whether the decision changes. Then inspect the correct explanation, identify the strongest distractor and describe what additional fact would make it more appropriate. Do not equate familiar wording or a remembered answer letter with flexible reasoning. The IES practice guide supports spaced learning and tests as learning tools; neither implies guaranteed examination performance.

theory.heading: Clinical calculation: planned and delivered
theory.text: An order specifies 1,200 mL of formula at 1.5 kcal/mL, delivered over 15 hours. Planned rate is 1,200 ÷ 15 = 80 mL/hour, and planned energy is 1,200 × 1.5 = 1,800 kcal. If a documented interruption means the formula runs only 12 hours at that rate, actual volume is 80 × 12 = 960 mL and actual energy is 960 × 1.5 = 1,440 kcal. Actual delivery is therefore 1,440 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 80% of the stated order. Check the clinical record, tolerance and care plan; a correct arithmetic answer does not authorize an unsupervised rate change.

theory.heading: Clinical context: a fact that changes the decision
theory.text: An adult with confirmed celiac disease asks about gluten-free bread prepared in a shared toaster used for wheat bread. The shared equipment is a plausible cross-contact risk, so identify a practical separation method and review the preparation process. Now change one fact: the person uses a dedicated clean toaster and separate utensils, but a seasoning ingredient is uncertain. Check the ingredient and other preparation steps rather than assuming the toaster remains the source. A symptom alone does not prove which exposure caused it. Nutrition decisions must account for the person’s preferences, adequacy and clinical context.

theory.heading: Management: when the denominator matters
theory.text: A meal service has $2,500 in food costs and $10,000 in food sales in the same period. Food cost percentage is $2,500 ÷ $10,000 × 100 = 25%; this is not a net profit percentage. Change food sales to $12,500 while food costs remain $2,500: the food cost percentage becomes 20%. Explain what stayed constant and what changed. Next consider a single-product break-even example: a price of $11 and variable cost of $6 leave $5 contribution per unit. With fixed costs of $500, the modeled break-even point is 100 units. These arithmetic models rely on their stated conditions and do not prove future demand.

theory.heading: Foodservice safety: read the entire standard
theory.text: The FDA 2026 Food Code is a model adopted or adapted by jurisdictions. For cooked time/temperature control for safety food, the cited cooling provision sets a maximum of two hours to cool from 135°F to 70°F and a maximum of six hours total to reach 41°F from 135°F. Finishing faster can meet these maximums; it is not wrong merely because it is faster. A case must specify the relevant starting point, intermediate temperature, elapsed times and applicable local rule. Do not infer that reheating always reverses the risk from an unsafe cooling history. When a question is based on another edition, identify the edition rather than combining values without checking.

theory.heading: Communication and evaluation across contexts
theory.text: Teach-back asks a learner to explain a plan in their own words so the educator can check the clarity of the explanation. Suppose an educator asks a patient to describe how they will compare serving sizes on two labels. A correct explanation shows understanding at that moment, not certain future behavior. Separately, in a community program, the number of sessions held is an output, while a specified change in participant behavior is an outcome. Match the measure to the objective. Across both cases, an easily counted activity does not automatically prove the desired change.

theory.heading: Practice the switch deliberately
theory.text: Write four column headings: clinical, education, management and foodservice. Under each, write one decision and one relevant datum. For clinical nutrition, distinguish the prescribed amount from what was delivered; for education, distinguish demonstration from later use; for management, specify both numerator and denominator; for food safety, identify the time, temperature and edition. Solve one short case in each column. Then switch their order and repeat without looking. If a mistake occurs, record whether it arose from a concept, reading condition, unit, arithmetic or uncertainty; this classification is a tool for your own review, not a conclusion about your overall ability.

theory.heading: Plan a new variation and a later revisit
theory.text: Choose one example that took effort and alter one meaningful feature while keeping the other assumptions fixed. For example, change the formula run time from 12 to 10 hours: at 80 mL/hour and 1.5 kcal/mL, delivered energy is 80 × 10 × 1.5 = 1,200 kcal. Check the result by first calculating volume, 800 mL, then multiplying by 1.5. Write the rule, the changed fact and the result. At the next review, try to reconstruct the reasoning before consulting the solution. A new case gives feedback about application; a few examples cannot establish official readiness or a scaled examination result.

worked_case.scenario: A meal service prepares cooked soup that cools from 135°F to 70°F in 90 minutes and from 135°F to 41°F in five hours total. In a separate nutrition-support case, a patient receives 800 mL of 1.5-kcal/mL formula. Under the 2026 FDA model code conditions described in this lesson, assess the cooling times and calculate delivered energy.
worked_case.reasoning: The first cooling interval is 1.5 hours, within the two-hour maximum; five hours total is within the six-hour maximum, assuming the stated measurements and applicable conditions. Faster cooling can satisfy a maximum. Separately, 800 mL × 1.5 kcal/mL = 1,200 kcal delivered. Do not use the soup times to assess the patient or the formula concentration to assess food safety. The applicable jurisdiction may adopt a different code edition; consult the local rule for real operations.

questions.stem: A patient receives 960 mL of formula providing 1.5 kcal/mL. How much energy was delivered?
options: 640 kcal
960 kcal
1,440 kcal
1,800 kcal
option_rationales: Dividing volume by concentration does not calculate delivered energy.
This would be correct only for a concentration of 1 kcal/mL.
Correct: 960 × 1.5 = 1,440 kcal.
This would be the energy in 1,200 mL at the stated concentration.

questions.stem: Under the stated FDA 2026 model cooling limits, soup goes from 135°F to 70°F in 90 minutes and from 135°F to 41°F in five hours total. Which statement is supported?
options: The described times meet both maximum limits, assuming the other applicable conditions are met
It fails because cooling faster than two hours is prohibited
It fails because the total time must always equal exactly six hours
Time does not matter if the soup looks safe
