option_rationales: Correct: 1.5 hours is within two hours and five hours total is within six hours.
These are maximums; faster completion is not prohibited by that reasoning.
Six hours is a maximum, not a required duration.
Appearance does not replace the time-temperature requirements.

questions.stem: Food cost is $2,500 and food sales are $10,000 in the same period. What is the stated food-cost percentage?
option_rationales: 20% would correspond to $2,000 out of $10,000.
40% would be $4,000 out of $10,000.
75% is the complement, not the requested cost percentage.

questions.stem: A person with confirmed celiac disease uses gluten-free bread in a toaster shared with wheat bread. Which issue warrants assessment?
options: Potential gluten cross-contact from shared equipment
A guarantee that the bread contains no contamination because it is labeled gluten-free
A requirement that every grain be avoided
Proof from the toaster alone that all symptoms have the same cause
option_rationales: Correct: shared equipment can transfer gluten-containing crumbs.
The labeled food can still be exposed during preparation.
Several grains and foods are naturally gluten-free; processing matters.
One possible exposure does not by itself prove the cause of every symptom.

questions.stem: Which action best uses teach-back after a patient receives a label explanation?
options: Ask the patient to explain in their own words how they will use the serving size
Count handouts and assume understanding
Require a verbatim recital as a pass/fail examination
Assume later behavior is guaranteed after one explanation
option_rationales: Correct: teach-back checks whether the explanation was clear.
Handout count is not a direct check of understanding.
The method is not a punitive verbatim test.
Immediate understanding does not guarantee later behavior.

questions.stem: A community program holds three classes and wants to measure whether participants later use a food resource. Which pair is correctly classified?
options: Three classes held: output; later resource use: outcome
Three classes held: outcome; staff funding: outcome
Later resource use: input; funding: output
Attendance: proof that the program caused a health change
option_rationales: Correct: delivered classes are an output, and later resource use can be an outcome.
Classes held are direct outputs; funding is an input.
Later use is an outcome, while funding is an input.
Attendance alone does not establish causation or a health outcome.

review: Return to Day 17: calculate delivered energy for 80 mL/hour over 10 hours at 1.5 kcal/mL and verify 1,200 kcal.
Return to Day 20: explain why 2026 FDA cooling times are maximums and why local adoption must be checked.
Return to Days 29–30: select a topic for a later new variation using actual evidence or a stated coverage-based fallback.

days.title: Timed Practice A
objectives: Practice a consistent decision process under a personally managed time limit.
Apply mixed-domain content to unfamiliar cases while documenting uncertainty.
Review explanations after practice without interpreting a small set as an official score.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Use 50 minutes for timed mixed practice and 40 minutes for review. During the first 25 minutes, work the original case below, its written variation and this day's five case questions; record your answer and a brief reason. Use the next 25 minutes for eligible mixed-domain questions already available under the app's domain practice. Set your own timer: this lesson does not start one automatically. Then spend 40 minutes reviewing the questions and explanations, particularly errors, guesses and slow decisions. Adjust the number of additional questions to the time available; do not rush the review or invent a score if you cannot complete a set.

theory.heading: What the app displays
theory.text: The practice questions on this lesson show correctness and explanations immediately after an answer is selected. If practicing timed decision-making, avoid studying the detailed rationale until the review period where practical; the visible correctness cue can still influence later answers. Record uncertainty before selecting, because the app does not provide a separate confidence setting on this page. Answers are stored on this device and cannot be changed within the lesson after selection; preserve them and use a new written variation for a retry. This is an exercise in pacing and reasoning, not a concealed or calibrated exam.

theory.heading: Choose a balanced, transparent practice set
theory.text: The 2022–2026 CDR outline assigns 21% to principles, 45% to nutrition care, 21% to management and 13% to foodservice systems. Use these proportions as a broad study guide where appropriate, not as a demand that a small practice set exactly match every percentage. For an exam from 2027 onward, check the applicable current CDR outline instead of assuming the old distribution applies. Flagged questions are excluded by the app from new sessions pending review; do not manually reintroduce them. Record which areas you actually practiced so an unrepresented topic is not mistaken for strong performance.

theory.heading: A repeatable decision process
theory.text: For each case, identify what action is being requested and the setting: assessment, intervention, monitoring, management or safety. Underline the unit, time period and qualifier that determine the answer. Separate what is observed from what is inferred. If an answer requires a fact not given, compare whether another option responds safely to the facts available. Use an estimate to detect a tenfold error before calculating. When two alternatives are plausible, name the fact that makes one more responsive to the question instead of eliminating one merely because it is longer. Record a brief reason when uncertain, then continue within your planned time.

theory.heading: Pacing is a skill, not a diagnosis
theory.text: At the start, decide how you will notice time without checking the clock after every sentence. If a case stalls, identify the needed information, make the best supported choice within the practice rules and note uncertainty. Do not infer a personal weakness from one slow or incorrect response: wording, units, unfamiliar context and fatigue can each contribute. The app's fixed practice blocks are not the official computer-adaptive exam. The CDR handbook explains the actual exam's variable question count and scoring; this 90-minute exercise is neither the official format nor a prediction of a passing result. No exam date is assumed.

theory.heading: How to use the 40-minute review
theory.text: Review all uncertain or incorrect answers first, then sample correct answers that took a long time. For each, note the decisive clue, your original reasoning, what the explanation and source support, and one changed-fact variation. Classify the likely issue as content, units, reading a qualifier or time management; treat that label as a hypothesis. If a source and answer key appear inconsistent, preserve the issue for review instead of forcing it into right or wrong. Distinguish a fact you can now explain from a result you only recognize. Choose a limited number of follow-up topics for Day 33 rather than opening a large new bank.

theory.heading: Worked timing and documentation exercise
theory.text: Suppose a learner spends 18 minutes on five original cases, including one uncertain response, and 27 minutes on additional mixed questions. Five minutes remain in the planned 50-minute practice block. They may record which areas were covered and the item that needs review, but should not assume that finishing early proves readiness. In the subsequent 40 minutes, they identify that a cooling question asked for total elapsed time, not time after the first measurement. They write the start and end times on a line and solve a new version. The outcome is an observable correction strategy, not an official scaled score. Write your own clock checkpoints before beginning and include breaks only within your available time.

worked_case.scenario: A service needs 15 lb edible, ready-to-cook vegetables. Its product-specific AP-to-EP yield is 75%. A patient reports falling intake, has new edema, and has a low albumin level during acute inflammation. A soup is recorded at 135°F at noon, 70°F at 1:45 p.m., and 41°F at 5:30 p.m.
worked_case.reasoning: Practice under your chosen timer: write the AP requirement, a next clinical assessment step and whether both named cooling limits are met. AP = 15 ÷ 0.75 = 20 lb before stock or package adjustments. The patient needs a fuller assessment of intake, weight history and relevant findings; albumin alone does not diagnose malnutrition and edema can obscure scale-weight changes. For FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14, the first stage took 1 hour 45 minutes and the total 5 hours 30 minutes, so the stated limits are met given valid measurements and applicable conditions. Change the final reading to 6:10 p.m.; the six-hour total is then missed. Record which fact decided each answer and check your reasoning after the timed block.

questions.stem: A serving has 140 mg sodium per 35 g on the label. How much sodium is listed for 70 g, ignoring label rounding?
options: 70 mg
140 mg
280 mg
490 mg
option_rationales: 70 mg divides the per-serving value by two instead of multiplying by two servings.
140 mg is the value for one 35 g serving.
Correct: 70 ÷ 35 = 2 servings; 140 × 2 = 280 mg.
490 mg does not follow from the specified serving size.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive nutrition-risk screen and edema. Which next action best supports an individualized plan?
options: Complete an assessment including intake, weight history and relevant clinical findings
Diagnose severity from the screen alone
Assume stable scale weight excludes tissue loss
Prescribe from albumin alone
option_rationales: Correct: screening signals risk and further assessment considers multiple findings.
A screening result alone does not establish a severity diagnosis.
Fluid accumulation can obscure scale-weight changes.
Albumin alone is not an accepted stand-alone diagnostic measure of malnutrition.

questions.stem: A foodservice operation needs 18 lb EP of a product with a verified yield of 90%. What AP quantity is needed before stock adjustment?
options: 20 lb
27 lb
option_rationales: Multiplying EP by yield reverses the calculation.
Adding 0.9 lb to the EP amount mixes a fraction and a weight.
Correct: 18 ÷ 0.90 = 20 lb AP.
The supplied yield does not yield 27 lb AP.

questions.stem: Under FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14, soup cools from 135°F to 70°F in 1.5 hours and reaches 41°F after 5 hours total. What do the recorded times show?
options: Both specified cooling limits are met
The first-stage limit was missed
The six-hour total was missed
Odor replaces the temperature record
option_rationales: Correct: 1.5 hours is within two hours and 5 hours total is within six.
The first stage is not longer than two hours.
The recorded total is less than six hours.
Odor does not replace time-temperature monitoring.

questions.stem: After an explanation, which request best uses teach-back?
options: Ask the person to explain the agreed plan in their own words
Ask only whether they understand and accept yes as proof
Repeat the instructions faster
Test whether they can use the same technical terms
option_rationales: Correct: an explanation in the person's own words helps check the clarity of communication.
A yes response alone does not demonstrate what was understood.
Speaking faster does not verify understanding.
Using technical language verbatim is not the goal of teach-back.

review: Review incorrect, guessed and slow items from the timed block, including any additional app practice; write one reason and one changed-fact variation for each priority.
Record which of the four domains appeared and which did not; do not infer readiness from missing coverage.
For the worked soup case, compute the elapsed time again using a number line and distinguish first-stage from total time.

days.title: Review Timed Practice A
objectives: Reconstruct the reasoning behind errors, guesses and slow decisions from Day 32.
Distinguish a knowledge gap from a unit error, missed qualifier or unsupported assumption.
Use source-backed variants to test whether a correction transfers to a new scenario.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes gathering yesterday's notes and revisiting Day 32 answers on the same device; 25 minutes reconstructing three decisions; 20 minutes working the examples and a changed-fact case; 20 minutes answering and reviewing today's questions; and 15 minutes choosing a small number of follow-up actions. If you used the app on another device, import the relevant backup first. The counts and categories below are examples, not a claim about your history.

theory.heading: Reconstruct before reading the explanation
theory.text: Choose an item you missed, guessed or answered slowly. Restate the question in one sentence: What decision did it request? Then write what you believed before looking at the rationale. Identify the given population, time period, unit, source edition and any qualifying phrase. Compare your initial answer with the correct option only after you can state the problem. A correct answer obtained by recall of its position still merits review. Conversely, a slow answer may reflect a difficult calculation rather than a permanent weakness. Record the actual evidence; do not assign personal deficits without repeated information.

theory.heading: Use a compact error analysis
theory.text: A useful review record has five fields: case or question identifier; the decisive clue; your original line of reasoning; the correction with a trustworthy source where needed; and a follow-up variation. For example, a learner reports that a cooling question was wrong because they subtracted the second-stage duration from the wrong start time. The correction is to mark the time when food reached 135°F, the time it reached 70°F, and the time it reached 41°F. The first interval must meet its limit and the entire interval must meet the total. A new case with different clock times checks the method more effectively than memorizing the original letter.

theory.heading: Do not let a source citation replace understanding
theory.text: A source is useful when it supports the specific claim, population and edition used in the question. The FDA 2026 Food Code is a model; local jurisdictions may adopt different versions or amendments. A USDA yield example applies to the stated product and preparation. ASPEN's fact sheet explains why albumin alone is unsuitable as a malnutrition diagnostic measure; that does not mean laboratory findings are never clinically relevant. If the answer or source is unclear, mark the item for further checking. Do not invent a missing source or calculate a performance percentage that treats a contested question as certainly correct or incorrect.

theory.heading: Distinguish four common sources of error
theory.text: Content: you did not know a concept and need a focused explanation. Calculation: you knew the relationship but used the wrong denominator, scale factor or rounding point. Interpretation: you missed a word such as total, minimum, before stock adjustment or during treatment. Timing: you used so much time on an early calculation that review suffered. More than one cause can occur, and language or unfamiliar wording may affect interpretation. For each item, select a tentative category and test it with a different example before deciding it is recurring. The response is an appropriate action, not a judgment of intelligence or a promise about the exam.

theory.heading: Worked review: edible portion and package rounding
theory.text: An exercise requires 27 lb of a specified usable product at a 75% verified yield. A learner multiplies 27 × 0.75 and chooses 20.25 lb AP. The direction is wrong: usable quantity equals AP × yield, so required AP is 27 ÷ 0.75 = 36 lb before stock. If 6 lb AP is safely available, the shortfall is 30 lb. If suppliers sell only whole 8 lb bags, four bags provide 32 lb. Three provide only 24 lb and do not meet the shortfall. On a new example, 21 lb EP at 70% yield requires 30 lb AP; at 5 lb stock and whole 8 lb bags, four bags are again needed for the 25 lb shortfall. The identical package answer does not make the intermediate quantities the same.

theory.heading: End with small, observable actions
theory.text: Prioritize no more than two topics that repeatedly affected reasoning or are not yet studied. For each, name the material to consult, a specific next task and a way to check it. Example: review the two cooling limits in the named FDA edition, write a timeline for one new case and explain the final decision. For an interpretation error, mark qualifying words before calculating; for a concept error, explain the mechanism using a different example. Do not use a single practice percentage as an official scaled score or a prediction of passing. Leave unresolved source conflicts and incomplete coverage visible in your notes.

worked_case.scenario: A learner chose 20.25 lb AP for 27 lb EP at 75% yield. On a cooling item, the learner measured only the time from 70°F to 41°F and ignored the start at 135°F. On a nutrition item, the learner considered low albumin alone sufficient to diagnose malnutrition.
worked_case.reasoning: First reconstruct the missing decisions. AP is 27 ÷ 0.75 = 36 lb, not 27 × 0.75. Under the cited 2026 FDA model, compare both the 135°F-to-70°F interval and the total 135°F-to-41°F interval with their limits. For nutrition, gather intake, weight and relevant clinical and physical findings; albumin can be affected by inflammation and does not alone diagnose malnutrition. Classify the first as a conversion-direction problem, the second as a missed time origin and the third as a conceptual error, subject to checking how the learner reasoned. Variation: for 24 lb EP at 80% yield, AP is 30 lb. Write a new cooling timeline and justify each endpoint.

questions.stem: A learner multiplies the required EP by a yield fraction to estimate the AP purchase. What is the best correction when the yield is usable EP divided by AP?
options: Divide required EP by the yield fraction
Multiply required EP by yield a second time
Add the yield percentage to pounds
Ignore the end form of the product
option_rationales: Correct: AP × yield = EP, so AP = required EP ÷ yield.
Repeating the same multiplication compounds the direction error.
A percentage fraction cannot be added directly to a weight.
The yield must match the specified product and end form.

questions.stem: For a 2026 FDA model cooling case, which review method best checks both limits?
options: Mark 135°F, 70°F and 41°F readings on one elapsed-time line
Review only time from 70°F to 41°F
Check only the refrigerator thermostat
Use odor in place of temperatures
option_rationales: Correct: the two-hour first stage and six-hour total share the starting temperature.
The second interval alone does not establish both required limits.
The equipment setting does not record food temperature over time.
Odor is not a substitute for the required time-temperature analysis.

questions.stem: A source linked to a question does not support its answer key. How should the learner record the item?
options: Flag it as unresolved and verify the source before scoring it as certain
Invent a justification for the key
Assume the citation makes every statement correct
Treat the disagreement as proof of personal weakness
option_rationales: Correct: source conflicts require checking before assigning a definite score.
A fabricated rationale does not resolve the conflict.
A link is not proof unless it supports the specific claim.
A questionable key is not evidence of a learner's persistent difficulty.

questions.stem: A learner solved a question correctly by remembering the letter from last time. Which follow-up best tests transfer?
options: Change the values and explain the reasoning
Repeat the same answer order only
Assume the full domain is mastered
Avoid reading any source
option_rationales: Correct: a changed-fact case requires applying the method rather than recognizing a letter.
The same order primarily reinforces recognition.
One remembered answer is insufficient to establish full domain mastery.
A relevant source can support or correct the reasoning.

questions.stem: An acute-illness case reports low albumin, but no intake or weight history. What is the best correction to the claim that albumin alone establishes malnutrition?
options: Collect and interpret multiple relevant assessment findings
Treat albumin as a stand-alone diagnosis
Assume a normal nutrition history
Wait for the illness to resolve before any assessment
option_rationales: Correct: intake, weight and other relevant clinical findings support assessment.
Albumin is affected by inflammation and is not alone an accepted diagnostic measure.
Missing history is not evidence of normal intake.
A needed assessment should not automatically be postponed.

review: Retrieve one Day 19 yield formula and check it using inverse multiplication.
Revisit one Day 20 cooling case using changed clock times; identify the first-stage and total intervals separately.
Write two follow-up actions based on actual reviewed items, without claiming weakness from a single observation.

days.title: Apply What You Reviewed
objectives: Apply reviewed rules to unfamiliar numbers and conditions across multiple domains.
Justify why the best option answers the specific question and why the nearest distractor fails.
Monitor repeated reasoning patterns without equating practice results with an official score.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 10 minutes retrieving the two priorities identified on Day 33; 25 minutes studying and explaining the examples below; 20 minutes solving the worked case and variations; 20 minutes answering and reviewing the original questions; and 15 minutes documenting the transfer check and a future review. These are authored practice cases, not official CDR items. Work the cases first; read explanations after recording your own reasoning.

theory.heading: Change the surface, keep the principle
theory.text: Transfer means using an established principle in a case that does not look identical to the one previously studied. A yield problem may ask how many pounds to buy, how much can be served from stock, or whether a stated order meets demand. Start with AP × yield = EP, then rearrange only as needed. For 28 lb AP at an 80% yield, usable EP is 22.4 lb; if instead 28 lb EP is required, AP is 35 lb. The same numbers have different meanings depending on which quantity is supplied. Confirm that the specified yield refers to the same product and preparation.

theory.heading: Vary one fact at a time
theory.text: Begin with a baseline case you can solve. Change one relevant value, timing detail or condition, then predict whether the answer should increase, decrease or require a different action. For example, if required EP stays fixed and yield falls from 80% to 75%, the AP needed increases. Check the prediction by dividing; do not rely solely on intuition. If a clinical vignette changes from no known edema to new edema, do not calculate an exact amount of tissue loss, but recognize that scale weight may now be more difficult to interpret. Describe the uncertainty and the additional data required.

theory.heading: Clinical follow-up must match the problem
theory.text: Imagine two patients report reduced intake. One describes difficulty obtaining food; the other describes nausea in hospital. A handout about a costly meal plan does not directly remove the first person's access barrier, and a purchasing referral alone does not treat the second person's symptom. Gather the person's goals and resources, coordinate relevant care, and choose an intervention linked to the assessed cause. Set a follow-up indicator that reflects the aim, such as intake and tolerance when those are the intervention targets. Albumin during acute inflammation is not a stand-alone malnutrition diagnosis or a sole measure of the intervention's effect.

theory.heading: Teach-back and evidence
theory.text: Teach-back checks whether information was communicated clearly by asking a person to explain or demonstrate what they will do in their own words. It is not a test of intelligence, and a person who cannot restate the plan has not proven noncompliance. The practitioner can explain in a different way and check again. Distinguish this communication process from a causal inference: an observation that intake improved after education does not alone rule out other changes. For a practical study check, write a plain-language question and identify which response would show that the step was understood.

theory.heading: Food safety with changed timelines
theory.text: Using the named FDA 2026 model, cooked TCS food must cool from 135°F to 70°F within two hours and from 135°F to 41°F or lower within six hours total. At 135°F at 9:00 a.m., 70°F at 10:50 a.m. and 41°F at 2:45 p.m., the intervals are 1 hour 50 minutes and 5 hours 45 minutes, respectively. Both specified limits are met if readings are reliable and other applicable conditions are satisfied. Change the final time to 3:10 p.m.: the total becomes 6 hours 10 minutes and the second limit is missed. Follow the site's corrective-action plan and applicable local requirements; do not infer a specific pathogen or rely on appearance.

theory.heading: Review both successful and unsuccessful transfer
theory.text: After each question, state the decisive fact, the principle and the calculation or action. For a correct response, explain why the most attractive wrong option fails; a remembered number without a reason may not transfer. For a wrong response, create a new variation and solve it independently. Keep a small note of repeated patterns, but avoid equating a few authored cases with a calibrated score. If a source conflicts with an answer or the setting is not specified, identify the uncertainty and verify it rather than inventing a universal rule. Record which domains were not represented in today's set.

worked_case.scenario: A service needs 22.5 lb of ready-to-use vegetables. The documented AP-to-EP yield is 75%, 6 lb AP stock is uncommitted, and the product is ordered in whole 8 lb bags. A client whose intake is low reports transportation barriers to food shopping. A separate cooling log starts at 135°F at 9:00 a.m., reaches 70°F at 10:50 a.m. and 41°F at 2:45 p.m.
worked_case.reasoning: AP requirement = 22.5 ÷ 0.75 = 30 lb; subtract 6 lb stock to obtain 24 lb, so three 8 lb bags are required. Explore feasible food-access options and a measurable intake goal with the client; a generic expensive recipe handout alone does not address the identified barrier. Cooling intervals are 1 hour 50 minutes and 5 hours 45 minutes total, within the two stated FDA 2026 model limits. Change yield to 50%: 22.5 ÷ 0.50 = 45 lb AP; after 6 lb stock the 39 lb shortfall requires five whole 8 lb bags. Explain why the order increased.

questions.stem: A menu requires 24 lb EP. The yield to the specified form is 80%, and 6 lb AP stock is usable. How much additional AP is needed before package rounding?
options: 24 lb
30 lb
36 lb
option_rationales: 19.2 lb multiplies EP by the yield rather than finding AP.
Correct: 24 ÷ 0.80 = 30 lb total AP; 30 − 6 = 24 lb to order.
30 lb is the total AP requirement before subtracting stock.
36 lb adds stock instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: A patient reports low intake because transportation to a grocery store is unavailable. Which response is most directly matched to the identified barrier?
options: Explore feasible food-access resources and follow up on intake
Only repeat an expensive recipe handout
Assume the patient is not motivated
Diagnose a condition without further assessment
option_rationales: Correct: it addresses the stated access barrier and includes monitoring.
A costly handout does not itself provide transportation or access.
The scenario does not establish motivation.
A diagnosis requires appropriate assessment rather than an assumption.

questions.stem: A patient cannot explain a new meal plan after the first instruction. Which teach-back response is most appropriate?
options: Explain the plan another way and ask the patient to describe it again
Label the patient noncompliant
Repeat the technical words more quickly
Assume the original explanation was fully understood
option_rationales: Correct: teach-back checks the clarity of communication and supports re-explanation.
Difficulty restating a plan is not proof of noncompliance.
Speaking more quickly does not check or improve understanding by itself.
The response indicates the explanation needs reassessment.

questions.stem: Under the FDA 2026 model, a batch starts at 135°F at 9:00 a.m., reaches 70°F at 10:50 a.m. and 41°F at 3:10 p.m. What is the result?
options: Both limits are met
The six-hour total is exceeded
The first-stage two-hour limit is exceeded
The readings prove the batch contains a specific pathogen
option_rationales: The total is 6 hours 10 minutes and exceeds six hours.
Correct: the final reading was ten minutes beyond the six-hour total.
The first interval is 1 hour 50 minutes, within two hours.
The timeline alone does not identify a specific organism.

questions.stem: When a source-backed practice item has an unclear answer because a required condition is missing, what best supports a reliable review?
options: Record the uncertainty and check the required condition before scoring
Guess a universal assumption and count it as certain
Memorize the answer's letter
Treat a missing condition as proof of a personal deficit
option_rationales: Correct: the omitted condition and supporting source need verification.
An unstated universal assumption may change the answer.
The letter does not resolve the underlying ambiguity.
An unclear question is not by itself evidence of a recurring weakness.

review: Revisit one Day 27 integrated case and change exactly one decision-relevant fact.
Explain to yourself why lower yield can increase the amount purchased for the same EP requirement.
Review one guessed or slow answer from the actual Day 32 session; write what evidence would show improvement in a new case.

days.title: Light Review and Pacing
objectives: Review pacing and reasoning using actual notes without treating a short session as a diagnostic test.
Apply a small number of changed-value cases and identify unfinished coverage.
Select manageable follow-up actions while accounting for fatigue and time.

theory.heading: Suggested 45-minute sequence
theory.text: Spend 8 minutes noting what was studied and how the recent sessions felt; 12 minutes working the case and one numerical variation; 15 minutes answering and reviewing the four questions; and 10 minutes choosing a manageable next action. If no timed session was completed, mark it as pending rather than inventing a result. This is a light review, not a new full-length test.

theory.heading: Observe process rather than predict a score
theory.text: Look at actual notes from Days 32–34, if available. Identify one decision that was slow, one explanation you can now state without a prompt, and one concept that still needs a source check. Consider whether difficulty arose from an unfamiliar topic, an omitted unit, a misread qualifier or limited time; these are hypotheses to test in new cases. A few questions and one 50-minute block do not measure endurance across an official exam. The CDR handbook, not the practice percentage displayed in an app, is the source for official exam administration details.

theory.heading: Choose a sustainable response
theory.text: If fatigue or schedule constraints interfere, adjust the next session rather than doubling the number of questions to compensate. Note one recovery or organization step and one focused study task. Return to the named sources for disputed claims. Keep categories such as not yet studied, studied with support and applied correctly to a new variation distinct. Evidence from several varied, reviewed items is more informative than answer recognition in one repeated question. The decision about exam readiness remains individual and cannot be guaranteed from this review.

worked_case.scenario: A learner completed 42 minutes of mixed practice and reviewed only two of several uncertain answers before time ran out. Another day they correctly calculate 16 lb EP at 80% yield as 20 lb AP, but cannot explain the direction of the conversion.
worked_case.reasoning: Record the unfinished review as pending and schedule time to complete it; do not label the learner unready based on one incomplete session. For the yield calculation, explain EP = AP × 0.80, so AP = EP ÷ 0.80, then reverse-check 20 × 0.80 = 16 lb. Try a variation: 26.4 lb EP at 80% yield requires 33 lb AP. A repeat correct answer should be accompanied by a defensible explanation. The two examples are illustrative and do not represent the user's history.

questions.stem: A learner did not complete review of several uncertain practice answers. What is the most useful next step?
options: Record the unfinished review and schedule time to complete it
Infer an official passing score from the number answered
Delete the unanswered history
Treat the unreviewed guesses as confirmed knowledge
option_rationales: Correct: the unfinished work remains visible and can be completed deliberately.
A short practice set does not produce an official scaled score.
Deleting history is not necessary to plan the next study action.
A guess requires reasoning review before it can support a knowledge claim.

questions.stem: A product yields 80% usable EP. How much AP provides 26.4 lb EP before stock adjustments?
options: 33 lb
40 lb
option_rationales: Multiplying by yield reverses the required calculation.
Adding 0.8 to the weight is not the yield relationship.
Correct: 26.4 ÷ 0.80 = 33 lb AP.
The stated numbers do not imply 40 lb.

questions.stem: What can one short timed practice block establish?
options: Some observations about decisions in that block, with substantial limits
A guaranteed passing result
Complete three-hour endurance
Mastery of all untested domains
option_rationales: Correct: a single short block is limited evidence about the observed tasks.
No such guarantee follows from a practice block.
A short block does not measure sustained performance across a longer session.
Untested domains cannot be established as mastered.

questions.stem: A learner repeatedly misses the word 'total' in elapsed-time questions. What targeted follow-up is most relevant?
options: Mark the starting and final times and solve a changed timeline
Memorize the option letter
Remove time units to simplify the question
Stop checking the time origin
option_rationales: Correct: a timeline makes the time origin and total interval explicit.
The option letter does not teach the method.
Units are essential for time comparison.
The time origin is necessary for the total interval.

review: Review the actual remaining notes from Day 33 or mark them pending; do not assume they exist.
Select one sustainable next action for Day 36 and one topic to revisit with a changed-fact case.
Record any source conflict for checking; do not treat this review as an official score.

days.title: More Demanding Mixed Cases
objectives: Identify the decision requested and data that materially change it in a multi-step case.
Distinguish suspected from confirmed disease and separate assessment from intervention and follow-up.
Compare plausible alternatives using source context and describe uncertainty rather than inferring exam readiness.

theory.heading: 90-minute session
theory.text: Study this lesson for 25 minutes, analyze the worked case for 15 minutes, answer the questions for 20 minutes, review every option and rewrite one case variation for 20 minutes, and complete spaced review for 10 minutes. All examples are fictional. Source links are optional for checking and deepening the core material on this page.

theory.heading: A structured first pass
theory.text: Long cases can combine symptoms, laboratory information, intake, a proposed intervention and a follow-up goal. First identify what the question requests: an assessment, immediate next action, calculation, teaching method or monitoring measure. Underline limiting words such as “confirmed,” “suspected,” “first,” “per serving,” “total time” and “under the stated model.” Next separate supplied facts from assumptions. A statement that a person is being evaluated for celiac disease is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis. A symptom or one laboratory value does not establish an entire clinical story. Then identify the fact that makes one action most appropriate at this point.

theory.heading: Suspected versus confirmed celiac disease
theory.text: NIDDK notes that beginning a gluten-free diet before diagnostic testing can affect test results. In a person being evaluated, coordinate testing and dietary decisions with the clinician rather than treating suspected disease as confirmed or giving an unsupervised diagnostic plan. For a person already confirmed to have celiac disease, wheat, barley and rye are gluten-containing grains; cross-contact can make a food unsafe even if the base food is gluten-free. A shared toaster or utensil can introduce crumbs. These two scenarios have different decisions: one asks how to coordinate a diagnostic workup; the other asks how to implement an established eating plan and prevent cross-contact.

theory.heading: Interpret a label without double counting
theory.text: A Nutrition Facts label’s added-sugars line is included in total sugars, rather than an additional quantity to add to the total. If one serving contains 14 g total sugars including 6 g added sugars, one serving has 14 g total, of which 6 g are added. For two servings, multiply each by two: 28 g total sugars including 12 g added sugars. Do not calculate 14 + 6 and then double it. The label calculation does not establish the person’s entire day of intake or a clinical diagnosis. Check the stated serving size and actual amount before comparing products.

theory.heading: A symptom requires assessment, not a reflex
theory.text: An individual receiving enteral feeding reports loose stools after a medication change. The formula, rate, medications, timing, other clinical conditions and fluid status may all be relevant. A temporal sequence raises a question but does not prove a specific cause. Review actual delivery against the order and coordinate assessment with the care team. Avoid assuming formula intolerance from one symptom or changing an order without the appropriate clinician. This reasoning remains valid if the trigger turns out not to be medication: the key is a documented assessment and proportionate action.

theory.heading: The closest plausible alternative
theory.text: After choosing an answer, state why another option might initially attract you and the missing or conflicting condition. Example: “Begin a gluten-free eating plan immediately” is plausible for confirmed celiac disease, but the scenario says the person is still being evaluated and asks about avoiding interference with testing. A choice to coordinate with the diagnostic clinician fits that stage better. In a follow-up question about a confirmed diagnosis, the appropriate decision may change. Never add an unmentioned fact merely to make an answer fit; if the stem leaves two truly defensible answers, mark it for source review.

theory.heading: Monitoring and outcome choice
theory.text: An intervention and its evaluation are distinct. If a patient agrees to compare the sodium in the usual amounts of two soups, a direct follow-up is to ask the person to perform the comparison with actual serving information or report the agreed action. The number of handouts printed is not a measure of that patient’s skill or behavior. Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words so the educator can clarify any misunderstanding. Correct teach-back at the visit does not prove later behavior or guarantee a clinical outcome. Choose a measure that matches the objective and time period.

theory.heading: Worked comparison: two food-label choices
theory.text: Product A lists 300 mg sodium per serving, and the person would eat two servings: 300 × 2 = 600 mg. Product B lists 450 mg per serving, and the person would eat one serving: 450 × 1 = 450 mg. For the stated amounts, B contributes 150 mg less sodium. Comparing only the per-serving figures would miss the usual amount eaten. This arithmetic does not make B appropriate for every person or address the rest of the day’s intake. Discuss accessibility, preference, overall nutrition and the individual clinical plan. To check transfer, exchange the serving amounts and calculate again before looking at the key.

theory.heading: A decision log without invented personal results
theory.text: For a mixed case, write four short lines: requested decision; decisive facts and missing data; reason for the selected option; reason the closest alternative is weaker. Include whether a source or edition was uncertain. If you have actual recent records, use them to select a later variation; if you do not, choose a topic based on unreviewed coverage and label that choice provisional. One difficult case is useful practice but cannot establish a personal weakness or a passing prediction. The goal is transparent reasoning under the conditions stated, not a memorized letter.

worked_case.scenario: A patient has recurring gastrointestinal symptoms and is discussing diagnostic testing for celiac disease with a clinician. They propose immediately eliminating gluten before the testing discussion. They also compare two soups: A lists 300 mg sodium per serving and they eat two servings; B lists 450 mg and they eat one. What should be clarified, and what is the sodium difference?
worked_case.reasoning: For the diagnostic question, recommend discussing testing and the dietary plan with the clinician before a self-directed change that could affect test results; suspected disease is not yet a confirmed diagnosis. Separately, soup A provides 600 mg and soup B 450 mg for the stated amounts, a difference of 150 mg. Do not treat the label calculation as proof of the diagnosis or a complete individual nutrition plan. Follow-up could ask the patient to demonstrate a comparison using their own usual amounts.

questions.stem: A person is being evaluated for possible celiac disease and plans to start a gluten-free diet before discussing diagnostic tests. What is the best next step?
options: Confirm celiac disease from symptoms alone
Discuss testing and the dietary plan with the diagnostic clinician before a self-directed change
Assume all blood tests remain equally accurate after eliminating gluten
Treat every gastrointestinal symptom as proof of gluten exposure
option_rationales: Symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.
Correct: a gluten-free diet before testing can affect results, so coordinate with the clinician.
NIDDK cautions that the dietary change can affect diagnostic testing.
Symptoms can have multiple causes.

questions.stem: A label shows 14 g total sugars including 6 g added sugars per serving. The person eats two servings. How much total sugar is listed for that amount?
option_rationales: 12 g is the added sugar in two servings, not total sugar.
This adds added sugar to total for one serving even though it is included.
Correct: 14 g total × two servings = 28 g, including 12 g added.
This double-counts added sugar before multiplying.

questions.stem: An enterally fed patient develops loose stools after a medication change. Which action best reflects the information supplied?
options: Assume the medication is definitely the cause and ignore fluid status
Review timing, medication, feed delivery, clinical context and hydration with the care team
Conclude that every formula is unsafe for the patient
Increase the rate without reviewing the order
option_rationales: Timing alone does not establish causation or remove the need to assess hydration.
Correct: multiple contributing factors and actual delivery should be assessed.
The symptom alone does not establish this universal conclusion.
The order and clinical status require review before changing delivery.

questions.stem: A person eats two servings of soup A at 300 mg sodium per serving or one serving of soup B at 450 mg. Which amount is lower for those stated portions?
options: A by 150 mg
B by 150 mg
The amounts are equal
B by 300 mg
option_rationales: A totals 600 mg and is not lower for the stated amounts.
Correct: A is 600 mg and B is 450 mg, a difference of 150 mg.
The stated totals differ by 150 mg.
The difference is 150 mg, not 300 mg.

questions.stem: For a patient with confirmed celiac disease, which kitchen practice is a plausible gluten cross-contact risk?
options: Using a toaster shared with wheat bread
Using a clean dedicated utensil
Checking a seasoning label
Separating gluten-free food during storage
option_rationales: Correct: gluten-containing crumbs can transfer in shared equipment.
A dedicated clean utensil helps reduce cross-contact.
Checking ingredients is a protective assessment step.
Separation helps reduce cross-contact.

questions.stem: The goal is for a patient to demonstrate a serving-size comparison. Which evaluation most directly matches it?
options: Count the number of handouts printed
Ask the patient to explain or demonstrate the comparison with a new label
Assume a nod establishes the skill
Measure the length of the waiting room
option_rationales: Handouts printed is a program output, not a direct demonstration of the skill.
Correct: observe or hear the requested skill with a new example.
A nod does not show the calculation or explanation.
Room length does not measure the objective.

review: Return to Day 16: distinguish testing for suspected celiac disease from management after confirmation.
Return to Day 23: use teach-back without treating the patient’s response as a pass/fail test.
Change soup B to 350 mg for one serving and calculate the difference from the stated 600 mg of soup A: 250 mg.

days.title: Calculations and Priorities Under Time Pressure
objectives: Set up clinical and management calculations with clear units and the correct denominator.
Distinguish the minimum whole purchase quantity from a fractional calculation when the question specifies indivisible units.
Apply a paced checking method while recognizing that arithmetic does not replace clinical or operational judgment.

theory.heading: 90-minute session
theory.text: Review the methods and examples for 25 minutes, work the case for 15 minutes, answer the mixed questions for 20 minutes, review every option and check calculations for 20 minutes, and complete spaced review for 10 minutes. A short timed attempt can help practice pacing; the study session includes the correction time. Values are hypothetical and do not describe personal performance.

theory.heading: A quick routine that preserves reasoning
theory.text: Read the final question before performing arithmetic. Write the requested unit, then note the supplied values, their units and relevant constraints. Estimate the direction and approximate size of the answer before using a calculator. Set up the operation and cancel units where possible. Check the result against the question: a number in mL is not kcal, and a total cost is not cost per unit. If the answer is implausible by a factor of ten, revisit decimal placement and unit conversion. A time limit is a practice constraint, not a reason to invent missing information or ignore safety.

theory.heading: Enteral energy, volume, rate and actual delivery
theory.text: Energy equals volume multiplied by formula concentration: mL × kcal/mL = kcal. Required volume equals prescribed energy divided by concentration. Rate equals volume divided by actual infusion hours. Suppose an order specifies 1,350 kcal from a 1.5-kcal/mL formula over 18 hours: 1,350 ÷ 1.5 = 900 mL, then 900 ÷ 18 = 50 mL/hour. Reverse-check: 50 × 18 × 1.5 = 1,350 kcal. If a documented interruption results in 16 actual hours at the same rate, delivery is 50 × 16 × 1.5 = 1,200 kcal. Do not assume an order proves delivery, and do not change a clinical prescription from arithmetic alone.

theory.heading: Protein and individualized assumptions
theory.text: When a clinical exercise supplies a target of 1.2 g/kg/day for a 75-kg individual, the amount is 75 × 1.2 = 90 g/day. The target is a supplied value, not a universal recommendation for all patients or diagnoses. A result in grams/day does not equal calories/day: if a separate question explicitly asks for protein energy using 4 kcal/g as its exercise factor, 90 g × 4 kcal/g = 360 kcal. The appropriate clinical target depends on the person and treatment; if no target is supplied or reliably identified, assess rather than inventing one.

theory.heading: Yield: purchased versus usable
theory.text: Edible portion (EP) is the usable quantity after the specified preparation; as-purchased (AP) is the quantity bought. With a supplied yield of 80%, producing 18 lb EP requires 18 ÷ 0.80 = 22.5 lb AP. Verify by 22.5 × 0.80 = 18 lb. If the supplier sells only whole pounds and the question asks for the minimum to meet the need, buy 23 lb; 22 lb would yield only 17.6 lb. If a question instead asks for the exact theoretical amount, 22.5 lb is the arithmetic result. Product cut, preparation and actual yield matter; use the specified data rather than assuming a universal yield.

theory.heading: Price, contribution and break-even
theory.text: Under a single-product model, unit contribution equals price minus variable cost. If price is $14 and variable cost is $8, contribution is $6. Fixed costs of $1,500 divided by $6 give 250 units at exact modeled break-even. With fixed costs of $1,501, the quotient is 250.167; if units cannot be divided, 251 is the minimum that avoids a loss in this model. Contribution is not net profit. Price, variable cost and fixed costs are assumptions for this calculation; changing volume, product mix or capacity can change the practical decision.

theory.heading: Time-temperature and the question’s boundary
theory.text: The FDA 2026 Food Code describes maximum cooling times for cooked time/temperature control for safety food: from 135°F to 70°F within two hours and from 135°F to 41°F within six hours total, under the relevant provision. If food reaches 70°F after 1.5 hours, the remaining time to meet the total six-hour maximum is 4.5 hours, not another six hours. Record actual times and temperatures and use the applicable jurisdiction’s adopted rule. A time that is faster than the maximum can comply; a faster first stage does not waive the total limit.

theory.heading: Accuracy under time pressure
theory.text: Consider a case asking for the minimum whole AP purchase. The exact quotient 22.5 lb is mathematically correct, but if only whole pounds are available it is not the requested purchasable quantity. Now compare a different item that asks for theoretical AP without a whole-unit constraint: rounding prematurely would lose information. Read the noun and unit in the prompt before choosing. For a multi-step question, mark which values are given and which were calculated. If the closest answer uses the wrong denominator or unit, write that reason explicitly rather than assuming it is incorrect simply because it differs from the key.

theory.heading: A paced practice and correction plan
theory.text: Practice a small, mixed set under a time budget while leaving time for correction. Record whether a delay came from locating a formula, interpreting language, setting units, calculation or uncertainty about the source; several causes can coexist. Rework an error without the key, then create one variation and verify it by inverse calculation. A shorter practice set cannot predict performance across a full examination or establish readiness. If no actual timing record is available, do not assume a pacing problem: use this as a general exercise and observe what happens on future attempts.

worked_case.scenario: A kitchen needs 18 lb usable cooked ingredient; a supplied conversion yield is 80%, and the supplier sells only whole pounds. Separately, an EN order calls for 1,350 kcal using 1.5 kcal/mL over 18 hours. Find the minimum purchase and the scheduled hourly rate.
worked_case.reasoning: For the kitchen, exact AP = 18 ÷ 0.80 = 22.5 lb. Because whole pounds are required, the minimum is 23 lb; 22 lb × 0.80 = 17.6 lb and is insufficient. For EN, volume = 1,350 ÷ 1.5 = 900 mL; rate = 900 ÷ 18 = 50 mL/hour. Reverse-check: 50 × 18 × 1.5 = 1,350 kcal. These are independent scenarios: the yield does not apply to formula delivery and the kcal concentration does not apply to the kitchen purchase.

questions.stem: An order specifies 1,350 kcal from a formula providing 1.5 kcal/mL, over 18 hours. What is the scheduled rate?
options: 40 mL/hour
50 mL/hour
75 mL/hour
112.5 mL/hour
option_rationales: 75 mL/hour for 18 hours at 1.5 kcal/mL delivers 2,025 kcal.
This does not follow from the prescribed volume and schedule.

questions.stem: For an exercise, a 75-kg patient has a clinician-supplied target of 1.2 g protein/kg/day. What is the amount?
options: 62.5 g/day
75 g/day
90 g/day
120 g/day
option_rationales: This divides rather than multiplies by the supplied target.
This assumes 1 g/kg rather than 1.2 g/kg.
Correct: 75 × 1.2 = 90 g/day; the target is specific to the exercise.
This would not equal the stated product.

questions.stem: A kitchen needs 19 lb edible portion with 80% yield. It can buy only whole pounds. What minimum purchase meets the need?
options: 19 lb
23 lb
24 lb
option_rationales: 19 lb AP at 80% yields only 15.2 lb.
23 lb AP yields 18.4 lb, below the need.
23.75 lb is the theoretical amount but is not a whole-pound purchase.
Correct: 24 lb is the smallest permitted whole amount that meets the need; it yields 19.2 lb.

questions.stem: A product sells for $14 with $8 variable cost per unit; fixed costs are $1,500. Under the single-product model, how many units provide exact break-even?
option_rationales: This uses the wrong denominator.
This uses $8 rather than the $6 contribution per unit.
This is not the quotient under the given model.

questions.stem: Under the cited FDA 2026 model cooling provision, food cools from 135°F to 70°F in 1.5 hours. How much of the six-hour total remains to reach 41°F?
options: Two hours
Three hours
Four and a half hours
Six additional hours
option_rationales: Two hours is the first-stage maximum, not the remaining total in this example.
Subtract 1.5 hours from six to calculate the remaining total.
Correct: 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 hours remain within the total maximum.
The total clock already includes the first 1.5 hours.

questions.stem: A calculation yields 22.5 lb required, but only whole-pound purchases are allowed and at least that amount is needed. Which is the best interpretation?
options: Buy 22 lb because rounding down is always correct
Buy 23 lb to meet the minimum constraint
Buy exactly 22.5 lb despite the stated restriction
Multiply the requirement by 100
option_rationales: Rounding down fails the minimum requirement.
Correct: 23 is the smallest allowed whole amount not below 22.5.
The question explicitly says fractional-pound purchase is not allowed.
This does not address the indivisible-unit constraint.

review: Return to Day 24: distinguish contribution per unit from net profit.
Return to Day 31: calculate 50 mL/hour × 16 hours × 1.5 kcal/mL = 1,200 kcal actually delivered.
Write one example where a question asks for exact theoretical quantity and another where it asks for a minimum whole purchase.

days.title: Remaining Content Gaps: Coverage and Verification
objectives: Build a coverage checklist without treating unattempted material or a small sample as proof of strength or weakness.
Distinguish reviewed, applied and uncertain content and select a feasible next action using available evidence.
Check source scope and test recall with a new case while preserving time for other domains.

theory.heading: 90-minute session
theory.text: Spend 15 minutes building a coverage map, 20 minutes studying one unreviewed or uncertain topic, 15 minutes on the worked case, 20 minutes on the practice questions, 15 minutes correcting and explaining each option, and five minutes scheduling a spaced revisit. The examples on this page are hypothetical and do not use personal history. The core lesson is self-contained; source links are optional for verification.

theory.heading: Coverage is not the same as mastery
theory.text: Create a checklist of the topics in the exam outline applicable to your intended exam date. Mark each topic as not yet reviewed, reviewed but not yet applied, applied on new examples, or uncertain/pending source review. These are descriptions of activity and evidence, not permanent judgments about ability. A topic with no attempts has unknown performance; it is not automatically a weakness or a strength. Marking a topic “reviewed” means that you encountered the material, not that you can reliably use it under every condition. Record the date and version of the outline rather than silently applying an old framework.

theory.heading: Use evidence proportionately
theory.text: If reliable records exist, list the number of new questions, correct responses, guesses and recurring reasoning issues for each subtopic. A small denominator or repeated exposure to the same item limits interpretation. For example, four correct responses out of four on the same memorized question are not four independent demonstrations. If records are absent, select an unreviewed topic as a coverage-based starting point. The 2022–2026 CDR outline gives domain weights of 21%, 45%, 21% and 13%; those proportions do not themselves identify an individual weakness or a passing score. Check the current outline for a later exam date.

theory.heading: Choose the next action
theory.text: Compare the remaining topics by whether they have been covered, relevance under the applicable outline, the quality and amount of actual evidence, and how much time is available. Choose one actionable subtopic, such as interpreting added sugars on a label or distinguishing output from outcome, rather than a vague goal to “master everything.” Write what the person should be able to do after review and how a new example will test it. Schedule a later revisit of another domain. If a recommendation is disputed or the question is ambiguous, record the uncertainty and investigate instead of forcing a score from an unreliable item.

theory.heading: Source scope, edition and jurisdiction
theory.text: A source should support the actual claim, population and context. Check the author, date, relevant section and whether the document is a guideline, model code, practice tool or patient-education page. The FDA Food Code is a model for adoption by jurisdictions, so a local rule and its edition should be checked for a real operation. A historical research finding or guideline can be appropriate if the question explicitly identifies its time frame; it should not be silently presented as the only current rule. If two sources differ, compare their populations, dates and assumptions. Do not average incompatible recommendations or modify an answer key by intuition.

theory.heading: Case variation: label literacy
theory.text: A label reports 10 g total sugars including 4 g added sugars per serving. For three servings, total sugar is 10 × 3 = 30 g, including 4 × 3 = 12 g added sugar. The 12 g are included in the 30 g; adding them again would double count. To apply the rule in a new case, change the serving count to two: 20 g total, including 8 g added. Explain the calculation in plain English and identify which quantity the question requests. This measures performance on the stated examples, not knowledge of every aspect of nutrition labeling.

theory.heading: Case variation: education and evaluation
theory.text: An educator wants to know whether a learner can compare the sodium in the portions they normally eat. Demonstrate the process and ask the learner to explain or perform it with a new label. The response can reveal whether the instruction was clear at that time. If the goal is later use, follow up on the agreed action and its barriers; a successful demonstration does not prove future behavior. In a program logic model, staff time is an input, a workshop is an activity, the number of workshops is an output, and a defined participant behavior can be an outcome. The measure must match the stated decision.

theory.heading: Diagnose the task, not the person
theory.text: After a practice question, distinguish what happened from an interpretation. “I divided the total by the wrong number of servings” describes a specific calculation. “I am bad at all nutrition math” is a sweeping claim unsupported by that one response. A difficult word, a missed qualifier, a unit error and a genuine concept gap call for different next steps; more than one may occur together. Define unfamiliar terms in English, rework the calculation with units, or return to the relevant source as appropriate. If the item itself lacks a necessary fact, mark it unresolved rather than blaming the learner.

theory.heading: Plan retrieval and a measured next step
theory.text: Write one rule without notes, verify it against the lesson, and answer a new variation after some time has passed. Space later practice while continuing brief review across other domains. Keep a small record: topic, source, date, number of new items, what happened, uncertainty and the next action. If you have only two new examples, say so; do not equate 2/2 with an official readiness determination. When a topic remains uncertain because a source is inaccessible or edition-specific, identify exactly what information is missing and continue another independent topic rather than fabricating a resolution.

worked_case.scenario: A hypothetical learner has no current exam history available. They have reviewed food labels but not applied the rule for added sugars; they have not reviewed the applicable foodservice outline. A label lists 10 g total sugars including 4 g added sugars per serving, and the patient eats three servings. How can the learner choose an action without labeling a personal weakness?
worked_case.reasoning: Record label content as reviewed but not yet applied, and foodservice as not yet reviewed; neither status establishes personal weakness. Apply the label rule: three servings contain 30 g total sugars, including 12 g added sugars. Write an explanation that avoids adding the included 12 g a second time, then try a new serving count. Choose a foodservice topic for a later coverage session using the outline relevant to the exam date. One example is limited evidence about a skill, not an official score or readiness prediction.

questions.stem: A topic has never been attempted, and no performance data are available. How should it be classified?
options: Demonstrated strength
Confirmed weakness
Coverage or performance unknown
Guaranteed mastery
option_rationales: No attempts provide no evidence of demonstrated strength.
No attempts do not prove weakness.
Correct: absent evidence leaves performance unknown; the topic may be selected for coverage.
No mastery can be guaranteed from absent data.

questions.stem: A label lists 10 g total sugars including 4 g added sugars per serving. A person eats three servings. How much total sugar is listed?
option_rationales: 12 g is added sugar for three servings, not total sugar.
14 g adds included added sugar to the total for one serving.
Correct: 10 × 3 = 30 g total, which includes 12 g added.
This double counts added sugar before multiplying.

questions.stem: A source and a question appear to disagree about a recommended value. What is the most useful first check?
options: Average both values
Compare population, source date, edition, and applicability
Assume the oldest source is always current
Delete the uncertainty without further review
option_rationales: An average might be supported by neither source.
Correct: differences in context or version can explain an apparent conflict.
Age alone does not establish current applicability.
Unresolved conflicts should be recorded and investigated.

questions.stem: A learner correctly answers the same memorized question four times. What does that establish?
options: Four independent demonstrations of transfer
Familiarity with that item; new variations are needed to assess application
An official passing score
That all other domains can be skipped
option_rationales: Repeated exposure to the same item is not four independent new cases.
Correct: a changed scenario provides more useful evidence about application.
An item history is not an official examination score.
One familiar item does not cover the other domains.

questions.stem: A workshop has occurred, and the program wants to assess a later participant behavior. Which measure best fits?
options: Number of workshops held
Whether participants report performing the specified behavior during the defined follow-up period
Number of chairs in the room
Number of staff members hired
option_rationales: Workshops held measure output rather than the later behavior.
Correct: the follow-up measure matches the population, behavior and time.
Chair count does not measure the behavioral objective.
Staffing is an input and does not establish the participant behavior.

questions.stem: A patient correctly explains a serving-size comparison during teach-back. What can the educator reasonably conclude?
options: The patient demonstrated understanding of the explanation at that moment
The patient will certainly follow the plan forever
Every clinical target has already been met
No practical barriers can exist
option_rationales: Correct: teach-back checks clarity and understanding in the current encounter.
Future behavior and access require follow-up.
One explanation does not prove all clinical outcomes.
Understanding does not eliminate barriers such as cost or access.

review: Return to Day 31: create one new case by changing a relevant fact and explain whether the decision changes.
Return to Day 22 or Day 30: distinguish one activity, one output and one outcome.
Choose one unreviewed topic from the applicable outline and record the selection as a coverage-based plan, not a diagnosed weakness.

days.title: Timed Practice B
objectives: Practice decision-making on new mixed-domain cases using a personally managed time plan.
Record uncertainty and review the reasoning behind each answer.
Compare practice sessions cautiously without treating them as an official exam or score.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Repeat the 50-minute practice and 40-minute review structure used on Day 32, if you completed it. For the first 25 minutes, solve the worked case, its variation and the five new authored questions below; note your reasoning and confidence before choosing an answer. Use up to another 25 minutes for eligible mixed-domain practice available in the app. Spend the remaining 40 minutes reviewing guesses, errors and slow decisions. Set your own timer: this lesson does not start one. Adapt the number of additional questions to available time rather than omitting the review. If you did not do Day 32, this can be your first timed practice.

theory.heading: Understand what the interface does
theory.text: The lesson reveals correctness and explanations as soon as you select an answer, and answers are saved on the current device. To preserve a useful review, record your reasoning and uncertainty before selecting; during the timed block, avoid studying detailed explanations until the review period where feasible. The visible feedback can still influence later choices. The lesson does not provide a concealed-answer exam mode or permit changing the selected answer after submission. To transfer lesson progress between devices, use the app's backup export and restore workflow. Do not clear site data to try to repeat a question; instead change the case facts and solve the variation in your notes.

theory.heading: Mixed practice and the 2026 outline
theory.text: The CDR 2022–2026 outline allocates 21%, 45%, 21% and 13% to the four domains, respectively. Use the distribution as a guide to broad coverage, while remembering that a small set cannot reproduce these percentages exactly. This lesson's five questions are original practice, not official CDR items. Domain-practice questions are study material and are not certified as exam questions; the separately labeled CDR practice set is distinct. Existing flagged items remain excluded from new sessions pending review. Do not turn their absence into a claim that all remaining items are certified. For an examination in 2027 or later, check the applicable official outline; the 2026 weights should not be carried forward automatically.

theory.heading: Decision sequence under time pressure
theory.text: Identify the requested task: calculate an amount, assess a patient, select an intervention, evaluate a program or interpret a control. Mark units, time origin and limiting words such as 'per serving,' 'total,' 'before stock adjustment' or 'under the stated model code.' Separate observed data from what still needs confirmation. Make an estimate before detailed arithmetic. Eliminate an option only when you can state why it conflicts with a fact or the scope of the question. If unsure, record the uncertainty before selecting and move on within your plan; do not interpret one uncertain answer as evidence of a persistent weakness.

theory.heading: Use valid comparisons
theory.text: If you practiced on Day 32, record how long each practice block lasted, the broad topic mix and whether the questions were new or previously seen. Compare similar conditions cautiously: different sources, item difficulty, topic mix and immediate feedback can make percentages non-comparable. Do not interpret a change of a few answers in a small set as proof of a trend. A practice percentage is not the official CDR scaled score. The CDR handbook describes official exam administration and scoring; this timed lesson is a study exercise and does not reproduce the actual exam environment or establish readiness.

theory.heading: Plan the review while practicing
theory.text: For every item, note the decisive clue and your first reason; mark those that were guesses, slow decisions or source conflicts. During the 40-minute review, start with safety-relevant uncertainties and unresolved sources, then examine the most attractive distractor for each priority item. Separate an error in concept from a unit conversion, misread qualifier, terminology or time-management issue. These categories are tentative: a single case cannot identify the cause reliably. Make a changed-fact version and check the method using the cited source or inverse calculation. Save a concise next step for Day 40 instead of repeating the same answer position.

theory.heading: Example: distinguish two time intervals
theory.text: Suppose soup starts cooling at 135°F at 10:00 a.m., reaches 70°F at 11:40 a.m. and reaches 41°F at 3:50 p.m. The first interval is 1 hour 40 minutes; the total is 5 hours 50 minutes. Under the named FDA Food Code 2026 model's standard cooked-TCS cooling provisions, both time limits are met, assuming valid readings and applicable conditions. If the final 41°F reading is at 4:10 p.m. instead, the total is 6 hours 10 minutes and the final limit is missed. The earlier first stage does not extend the total. Write the times on a line rather than subtracting only the second interval.

worked_case.scenario: An operation needs 27 lb EP of a specified produce item at 90% verified yield. It has 5 lb AP of usable, uncommitted stock and buys whole 6 lb bags. In a separate case, a patient has a positive risk screen and edema during an acute inflammatory illness; no intake history has yet been obtained.
worked_case.reasoning: Before selecting an answer, calculate 27 ÷ 0.90 = 30 lb AP total. After subtracting 5 lb stock, the shortfall is 25 lb; five 6 lb bags provide 30 lb and four provide only 24 lb. The clinical screen identifies possible risk and prompts further assessment; obtain intake, weight history and other relevant findings. Edema may obscure weight change, and a lab value during inflammation alone does not establish malnutrition. Variation: if usable stock is 12 lb AP, the 18 lb shortfall requires three bags. Write the two calculations and one missing clinical fact before checking the questions.

questions.stem: A packaged food lists 180 mg sodium per 60 g serving. What amount is listed for 150 g, ignoring label rounding?
options: 270 mg
360 mg
450 mg
540 mg
option_rationales: 270 mg represents 1.5 servings rather than 2.5.
360 mg represents 2 servings, or 120 g.
540 mg represents 3 servings.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive nutrition-risk screen and newly reported reduced intake. What is the best next step?
options: Complete an individualized nutrition assessment
Assign severe malnutrition solely from the screen
Assume intake is normal until albumin falls
Use the same plan for every patient
option_rationales: Correct: screening identifies risk and supports further assessment.
A screen alone does not establish a diagnosis or its severity.
Reported intake needs assessment; albumin need not fall first.
A plan must reflect the person's findings and context.

questions.stem: A service needs 24.3 lb EP of a specified product with a verified yield of 90%. Before stock adjustments, what AP amount is required?
options: 27 lb
36 lb
option_rationales: Multiplying EP by yield reverses the needed conversion.
Adding the decimal yield to pounds mixes unlike quantities.
Correct: 24.3 ÷ 0.90 = 27 lb AP.
The stated quantity and yield do not require 36 lb.

questions.stem: Under FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14, soup reaches 70°F 1 hour 40 minutes after reaching 135°F and reaches 41°F at 6 hours 10 minutes total. Which limit was missed?
options: The first-stage limit
The six-hour total limit
Neither specified limit
The timeline proves a specific pathogen
option_rationales: The first stage is less than two hours.
Correct: the final temperature is documented after the six-hour total.
The final total exceeds the stated limit.
A time deviation alone does not identify a specific organism.

questions.stem: A team tries a small change in a meal-service process and compares results with its prediction. What is the most appropriate next use of the information?
options: Study the result and decide whether to adapt and test again
Assume the first result proves causation under every condition
Discard all records after collecting them
Ignore the prediction and outcome
option_rationales: Correct: a PDSA cycle uses the observed result to inform the next action.
One small test does not prove causal effects under all conditions.
Records can support learning and evaluation.
The comparison is central to interpreting the test.

review: Review this day's guesses, errors and slow decisions, including any additional app practice; identify the fact or assumption that determined each answer.
If Day 32 data are available, compare topic mix and conditions before interpreting any difference; if not, mark comparison pending.
For a foodservice problem, solve a changed-yield example and verify the result by multiplying AP by yield.

days.title: Review Timed Practice B
objectives: Reconstruct decisions from the actual practice session, including correct but uncertain choices.
Distinguish evidence gaps from arithmetic, reading or pacing issues without assuming a deficit.
Design a specific source-backed variation and follow-up for each selected issue.

theory.heading: Suggested 90-minute sequence
theory.text: Use 10 minutes to collect Day 39 answers and notes, if available; 25 minutes to reconstruct three selected decisions; 20 minutes to work the integrated case and new variations; 20 minutes to answer and review today's questions; and 15 minutes to document the next review. If no prior session exists on this device, mark it pending and use the illustrative case rather than inventing results. Lesson answers can be transferred via the Profile backup export and restore process.

theory.heading: Review the process before the letter
theory.text: Select an actual item that was incorrect, guessed or unusually slow, if one exists. Before reading the explanation again, write the requested decision and the information you used. Identify a time boundary, unit or qualifier that mattered. For a correct but guessed answer, reconstruct why it is correct and why the closest alternative is less suitable. Do not assume that an incorrect answer proves lack of knowledge or that a correct answer proves mastery. The recorded reasoning and a new variation are more informative than the letter alone.

theory.heading: A structured review record
theory.text: A compact record can contain: item or case ID; selected answer; confidence or uncertainty as recorded before feedback; decisive clue; initial reasoning; source-backed correction; and a changed-fact follow-up. Mark whether a source conflict or missing condition prevents confident scoring. These are study notes, not clinical records or an official score report. If you used additional app practice, review its explanations separately and note which items were actually encountered. Do not paste private patient information into notes; use fictional or de-identified details appropriate to your setting.

theory.heading: Sort possible causes, then test the hypothesis
theory.text: A content issue may require a focused source review; a calculation issue may need units, an inverse check and practice with new values. A reading issue may involve missing 'total,' 'minimum' or 'within'; a timing issue may reflect how time was distributed. The same response can have more than one cause. Suppose a learner calculates a 25 lb purchase shortfall correctly but orders only four 6 lb bags. The likely issue is whole-package rounding, but confirm the learner's reasoning before assigning that cause. Rework the problem: four bags supply 24 lb; five supply 30 lb. Then change the shortfall and solve again.

theory.heading: Source, edition and setting
theory.text: A citation should support the precise statement and the context used in a question. The USDA Food Buying Guide example concerns a particular product and yield form; do not use it as a universal yield for all produce. The FDA Food Code 2026 is a model; the adopted local rules may differ. ASPEN's guidance notes that serum albumin is affected by inflammation and is not alone an accepted malnutrition diagnostic measure. A source link is a starting point for checking, not a guarantee that every statement in an explanation is correct. Preserve unresolved conflicts for further review instead of scoring them as certain.

theory.heading: A worked review of a cooling timeline
theory.text: Suppose food starts cooling at 135°F at 8:00 a.m., reaches 70°F at 9:30 a.m. and reaches 41°F at 2:20 p.m. The first interval is 1 hour 30 minutes, but the total is 6 hours 20 minutes. Under FDA Food Code 2026 §3-501.14, the total limit was missed even though the first stage was timely.
